sentences: Swimming is one of the most complete sports.

In the water, the body is lighter.
That's why this sport is suitable for almost everyone: children, elderly people, and those with back pain.
Swimming is also good for the mind.
Many people say that after a few laps, they feel calmer.
The sound of the water, the regular rhythm of the movements: all of this helps to forget the worries of the day.
You can start at any age.
It's never too late to learn to swim.
The only real advice is consistency.
Swimming once a month is useless; twice a week makes all the difference.

sentences: Our time has made speed a cardinal virtue.
Everything must go faster: meals, transportation, exchanges, careers.
A message demands an immediate response; a queue becomes a small suffering; a page that takes two seconds to load frustrates us.
We measure the value of things by their speed, and slowness has become, at best, a weakness, at worst, a fault.
It is against this rarely questioned obviousness that a discreet movement has emerged, born in Italy at the end of the 1980s, around a simple idea: what if we are going too fast?
We would be wrong to see it as a mere whim of nostalgic privileged people.
Certainly, slowing down often requires a certain comfort, and it would be indecent to preach slowness to those juggling jobs to survive.
But the central idea of the movement touches on something universal, which goes beyond the question of means.
Here it is: speed destroys what it claims to give us.
Let's take a meal.
Swallowed standing up in five minutes, it fills the stomach but nourishes nothing else; we remember neither its taste nor that moment.
Taken slowly, shared, savored, the same meal becomes an experience, a pleasure, sometimes a lasting memory.
Speed may have saved time — but it has eliminated the essential, which was precisely in the time spent.
What holds for the meal holds for almost everything: a rushed conversation, a landscape crossed without seeing it, a book skimmed through.
By going faster, we do more things, and we experience less.
There is a paradox here that slowness illuminates.
We run to gain time, but this gained time, we immediately fill with other tasks.
Speed is never satisfied; the faster we go, the faster we need to go again.
We save ten minutes only to swallow them up in ten new tasks, and the feeling of lacking time, far from decreasing, worsens.
He who has always run never arrives.
Would he be mistaken, however, the one who concludes that everything must be done slowly?
Certainly.
Living in slow motion would be as absurd as living at full speed, and often impossible in the world as it is.
Well-understood slowness is not a uniform rule; it is an art of discernment.

It is not about slowing everything down, but about choosing: identifying the moments that deserve our time — a family meal, a walk, an important conversation — and protecting them from the surrounding haste.
For the rest, speed retains its rights; no one demands to daydream while paying their bills.
Ultimately, true wealth may not be about doing a lot, but about fully living the little that matters.
Slowing down is not wasting your time.
It is refusing to let your life slip by without having lived it.

sentences: In the act of traveling, there is something irrational that our habits prevent us from seeing.
We work hard, we save money, and then we spend that money to leave a comfortable home to sleep elsewhere, often in worse conditions, at the cost of fatigue, waiting in lines, and discomfort.
We pay to lose our bearings.
From a distance, this behavior seems strange.
It must therefore respond to a deep need.
Which one?
The most immediate answer is escape.
Escaping routine, first — that dull weariness of daily life, where the days resemble each other to the point of blending together.
Travel breaks the repetition; it reintroduces the unexpected, novelty, and surprise, sensations that ordinary life, through regularity, ends up stifling.
This is no small matter: many people live an entire year for two weeks that will be etched in memory, precisely because they break the mold.
Travel is a condensed version of life, where the daily routine can sometimes feel like a diluted existence.
But to limit it to escape would be to miss the essential, because travel is not just a subtraction — it is also an addition.
By discovering other countries, we mainly discover other ways of being human: different ways of eating, greeting, working, and perceiving time, family, and happiness.
This encounter has a precious and subtle effect: it puts our own habits into perspective.
What we took for the natural order of things — our schedules, our codes, our certainties — turns out to be just one possibility among others.

Travel may be the best remedy against narrow-mindedness: it's hard to believe that your way of living is the only right one when you've seen, with your own eyes, a thousand different ways to live well.
Finally, there is a more intimate dimension that we are less willing to admit.
Travel not only makes us meet others; it also helps us meet ourselves.
Torn from our bearings, deprived of the familiar gaze that fixes us in a role, we find ourselves acting differently.
The shy person dares to speak to strangers; the hurried one takes their time; we discover ourselves to be braver, more curious, or more fragile than we thought.
Far from home, without our usual audience, we are a little more ourselves — or we glimpse another possible self.
That's why so many people return from a trip with the feeling, hard to explain, that they have changed.
Then a troubling question remains.
If travel is primarily valuable for the inner journey it produces, do we really need to go to the ends of the earth to achieve it?
Some have noted with irony: you can travel across continents without seeing anything, locked in your habits and your phone, and conversely, you can rediscover your own city with fresh eyes.
True travel may not be about kilometers, but about openness — this ability to open up, to be amazed, to let oneself be moved.
"We travel to see the world," they say.
That's true, but incomplete.
We also travel, and above all, to see ourselves in a different light, and to return — because we must return — a little different from the person who left.

sentences: Since the pandemic, many people are working from home, which means they work at home instead of going to the office.

The morning of working from home is pleasant.
No commuting, no crowded subway.
I enjoy my coffee quietly and turn on my computer.
But be careful: working at home requires discipline.
The hardest part is concentrating.
At home, there are a thousand distractions: the television, the fridge, the laundry.
You really have to get organized.
I always sit at the same table, as if it were my office, and I make a list of my tasks for the day.
Of course, I'm not alone.
Thanks to the screen, I stay in touch with my colleagues.
We often have video conference meetings.
It's not like in the office: sometimes the connection is bad, and everyone talks at the same time!
But you get used to it.
The real danger of working from home is balance.
When work is at home, you never really stop.
In the evening, I'm sometimes tempted to reply to one last message.
So I made a decision: at six o'clock, I shut down my computer and I don't open it again.
Working from home has its advantages and disadvantages.
I like the freedom it gives me, but I also need to see my colleagues in person.
That's why the balance between the two suits me perfectly.

sentences: We often imagine that saving means depriving oneself: giving up pleasures, counting every penny, and leading a sad life.
This is a mistake.
The people who save most effectively are not necessarily the stingiest; they are the ones who know how to distinguish between a desire and a need.
The difference seems obvious, but it isn't in real life.
A need is what is necessary: having a place to live, eating, getting around.
A desire is what would feel good in the moment: the latest phone, one more piece of clothing, an item seen in an advertisement.
The problem is that modern marketing constantly works to turn our desires into needs.
It convinces us that we cannot live without what we didn't even know we needed yesterday.
Resisting this trap doesn't require iron willpower, but a few simple habits.
The most effective one is to wait.
When faced with a desire to buy, we give ourselves a few days before deciding.
Very often, the desire disappears on its own: we had confused a fleeting wish with a real need.
The money saved this way does not represent any sacrifice, since we don't regret what we didn't buy.
Another key is to ask the right question.
Not 'Can I afford it?', but 'What value will this purchase really bring me?'.
Some expenses, even significant ones, enrich life: a trip, a book, a shared meal.
Others, once the excitement has faded, leave just one more object in a closet.
Saving intelligently, therefore, is not about saying no to everything.
It's about saying yes to what matters and no to what doesn't.
Seen this way, saving stops being a deprivation and becomes a form of freedom: the freedom to no longer spend by reflex and to keep our money for what truly has value for us.

The storm lasted an hour.

The office was small.
There was no one there, except for an employee behind a counter.
"Hello, I lost an umbrella on the tram Monday evening."
"Which line?"
"Line B."
He wrote something down, then he disappeared into a room behind him.
While he was searching, I looked through the open door.
That room was amazing!
There were shelves from floor to ceiling, filled with objects: bags, coats, books, glasses, toys.
There was even a guitar.
The employee came back with three umbrellas.

Black, with a wooden handle.

The children were a little scared, so we told stories.

One neighbor had a chainsaw, another had a trailer.
We worked together for four hours to clear the road.
I didn't know half of these people.
The electricity came back in the evening, after six o'clock.

sentences: Three months ago, I hurt my back.
It happened stupidly, while carrying a box of books.
I bent my back instead of bending my legs.
I felt a sudden pain, like an electric shock, and I couldn't move for a few seconds.
The next day, it was worse.
I couldn't put on my socks by myself.
My doctor examined me and reassured me: it wasn't serious.
"You have a blocked muscle.
It will take one or two weeks."
He gave me medication and a surprising piece of advice: "Don't stay in bed.
Move gently."
I thought you had to rest completely.
He explained the opposite to me: staying lying down too long made the problem worse.
He also sent me to a physiotherapist.
The physiotherapist showed me simple exercises to do every morning.
But above all, he asked me questions about my daily life.
How many hours did I spend sitting?
About nine hours a day.
"That's the real problem," he said.
"The box was just the last straw.
Your back is weak because it never moves."
Since then, I've changed two things.
I get up every hour at the office, and I walk for twenty minutes each day.
I no longer have back pain.

sentences: Last month, my father almost lost a lot of money because of a phone scam.

He said he worked at my father's bank, in the security department.

He spoke politely and calmly.
He explained that a suspicious transaction had just been detected: someone was trying to withdraw one thousand eight hundred euros.
We needed to act right away.
He asked my father to confirm his card number and to provide the code received by SMS.
My father was worried.
The man spoke quickly and kept repeating that it was urgent.
But just before giving the code, my father remembered one thing: a real bank never asks for a code over the phone.
So he said, "I'm going to hang up and call my bank myself."
The man immediately changed his tone and became aggressive.
My father hung up.
He called his bank using the number written on his card.
There was no suspicious transaction, of course.
Urgency is the main weapon of these scammers.
They don't want us to think.
Since then, my father has a rule: he always hangs up and calls back himself.

sentences: A few years ago, I bought a pair of shoes for thirty euros.
They lasted seven months.
I bought a similar pair, then another one.
A friend then explained a very simple calculation to me that changed the way I shop: the cost per use.
Thirty euros for seven months of daily wear comes to about fourteen cents a day.
A pair that costs one hundred twenty euros and lasts five years amounts to seven cents.
So the 'expensive' pair actually costs half as much.
This reasoning doesn't apply everywhere, and it shouldn't be made an absolute rule.
A high price does not guarantee quality at all: in many sectors, you mainly pay for a brand.
So you need to look at the manufacturing, the warranty, and the possibility of repairs.
It also assumes you have the money upfront, which is far from the case for everyone.
Not being able to buy durable items and having to constantly replace them is one of the most concrete ways that a lack of money is costly.
But when the choice is available, the useful question is not 'how much does it cost?'.
It is: 'how long will it last, and can I get it repaired?'
I have applied this logic to only a few items: shoes, a coat, a pot, a bag.
They cost me more at the start.
I still have all of them.
And curiously, I pay more attention to them.
We take better care of what we don't plan to replace.

sentences: Many adults make the same observation: it is significantly harder to make new friends at thirty-five than at eighteen.
This is often explained by personality — people have supposedly become less open and more difficult.
The explanation is probably elsewhere, and it is more reassuring.
Sociologists identify three conditions that promote the formation of a friendship: repeated proximity, unplanned interactions, and an environment that encourages lowering one's guard a bit.
At school or university, these three conditions are constantly present, without any effort.
You see the same people every day, you run into each other without planning it, and you share a common situation.
In adulthood, they almost all disappear.
You often see your colleagues, but in a professional setting that limits what you show of yourself.
Meetings become planned: you have to suggest a date, postpone it, reorganize.
And the unexpected, which creates connections, becomes rare.
This diagnosis has the advantage of being actionable.
If friendships arise from repetition, then what works is regular activity: a weekly class, a sports club, a community engagement, a choir.
Not because the activity matters, but because it recreates frequency.
A single dinner rarely produces a friendship.
Twelve sessions of the same activity often do.
The other lever is less comfortable: you have to dare to propose.
In adulthood, someone has to make the first move, and everyone is waiting for the other to do it.
It's not intrusive.
In most cases, the person opposite is simply relieved.

sentences: We talk about forgetting as a flaw: 'I have a bad memory.'
Researchers describe it more as a function.
A brain that remembered absolutely everything would be unmanageable.
Forgetting sorts: it eliminates what hasn't been useful, leaving accessible what is often needed.
The problem is that this sorting doesn't always match our intentions.
Studies on memory have highlighted a pattern known as the forgetting curve.
After learning something, we lose a large part of it very quickly — often the majority in the first few days — and then the loss slows down.
This curve explains a familiar experience: cramming the night before an exam allows you to pass the exam, but you forget everything three weeks later.
But it also indicates the solution.
Every time we retrieve information just before forgetting it, the curve flattens: forgetting becomes slower.
This is the principle of spaced repetition.
We review a concept after one day, then three, then one week, then one month, spacing it out gradually.
This method seems counterintuitive because it is less comfortable.
Rereading your notes gives a sense of mastery; testing yourself, on the other hand, highlights what you don't know.
It's unpleasant, and that's precisely what works.
The most effective vocabulary apps all rely on this principle.
The principle applies beyond languages: for a course, a professional procedure, a piece of music.
It's not about working more.
It's about working at the right time.

sentences: Every day, we see a very large number of images of human bodies.
Almost all of them are selected, framed, retouched, lit, and sometimes automatically modified by a filter.
This is not new — advertising has been retouching for a long time — but the scale has changed.
The phenomenon now involves photos of ordinary people, and filters are applied in real time, often by default.
Research in social psychology shows a constant mechanism: we compare ourselves to what we regularly see, without deciding to do so.
When the point of comparison is a set of optimized images, the comparison is systematically unfavorable.
Documented effects include increased body dissatisfaction, particularly among teenage girls, but not only: young men are increasingly affected, with an equally unattainable muscular ideal.
It would be simplistic to make it a question of vanity.
A degraded self-image influences concrete behaviors: avoiding certain activities, giving up the pool, adopting unbalanced diets, or conversely, abandoning all sports out of discouragement.
What can we do?
Effective approaches do not consist of asking people to 'accept themselves' — an easy and ineffective injunction.

What works better: diversifying what we see by following accounts showing varied and unretouched bodies; reducing exposure to content that triggers comparison; and shifting attention from appearance to function.
This last idea deserves to be emphasized.
A body that walks, carries, swims, or dances does something.
It is a fairer and more sustainable criterion than its appearance in a photograph.

sentences: Retirement is one of the few events that people anticipate for decades.
People look forward to it, calculate it, and talk about it.
And yet, some new retirees describe a difficult period, usually six to eighteen months after stopping work.
This phenomenon is documented.
The first few months often feel like a long vacation: you sleep, fix what you had left undone, and travel.
Then comes a more delicate phase, when this list is exhausted.
Three losses combine, rarely anticipated.
The first is the structure of time.
A job imposes a rhythm: schedules, deadlines, and different days.
Without it, the days look the same, and many retirees say they were surprised by this lack of reference points.
The second is the social network.
A large part of an adult's daily relationships comes through work.
They often fade away in a few months, without conflict, simply because the connection was contextual.
The third is the perceived usefulness.
Being expected somewhere, having a role, creates a feeling that rest does not replace.
Those who navigate this transition well have generally planned something other than just stopping: a volunteer activity, training, community engagement, or regular childcare for grandchildren.
The common point of these activities is that they provide rhythm, relationships, and a form of responsibility.
A former colleague summarized it for me after two years of retirement:
"I thought I wanted to do nothing."
"In reality, I wanted to choose what I do."

sentences: People often answer the question, 'What is the purpose of school?' with an obvious response: to transmit knowledge.
This answer is correct, but incomplete, because school serves multiple functions at once, which do not always align.
The first function is indeed the transmission of knowledge: reading, writing, counting, understanding the world.
This is the most visible mission.
The second function is socialization.
At school, a child learns to live with people they haven't chosen, to respect common rules, to wait their turn, to cooperate, and to handle disagreement.
These lessons are not included in any curriculum, but they are among the most lasting.
The third function is less frequently stated: selection.
School guides, classifies, and awards diplomas that open or close doors.
This function is necessary — we need to organize access to training — but it sometimes conflicts with the other two.
This tension is real.
A system obsessed with selection risks reducing learning to measurable performance, to the detriment of curiosity.
Conversely, a system that neglects evaluation deprives students of benchmarks and can hide difficulties until it's too late.
This debate runs through all educational reforms in every country.
It explains why these reforms are so difficult: they do not resolve a technical problem, but a disagreement about what school should prioritize.
Most people actually want all three functions at once.
The problem is that they sometimes pull in opposite directions.

sentences: It is almost impossible to walk through a French village without encountering a war memorial.
There are tens of thousands of them.
This presence, so ordinary that we no longer pay attention to it, deserves a moment of pause.
The vast majority of these monuments were erected after World War I, between 1920 and 1925.
They bear the names of the local residents who were killed during the conflict.
What strikes you when you read these lists is their length, even in very small villages.
Some municipalities with just a few hundred inhabitants have several dozen names.
You often find the same last name repeated: brothers, cousins, who fell just a few months apart.
This war killed about one and a half million French soldiers in a country of forty million inhabitants.
Almost every family was affected.
This explains the momentum that led so many municipalities, even the smallest ones, to build a memorial.
These monuments are not just lists.
They carry messages that reveal the mindset of the time: patriotic pride, but also, in some cases, a rejection of war, which is rarer and braver.
Every November 11th, a ceremony takes place there.
Today, it attracts fewer people than before, as the direct memory fades.
This raises a question: what to pass on when there are no more witnesses?
The last combatants of this war have been dead for a long time.
What remains are the stones, and the names engraved on them.
Reading them aloud, just once, is often enough to understand why these monuments exist.

sentences: Among urban pollutants, noise is probably the most underestimated.
It is seen as an annoyance, a discomfort, rarely as a health problem.
The data says otherwise.
Constant noise — traffic, construction, activities — has measurable effects on the body, regardless of the irritation it causes.
It disrupts sleep, even when we think we've gotten used to it.
It keeps the body in a slight state of alertness, which, over the long term, increases tension and cardiovascular risks.
This last point is counterintuitive.
We think we get used to noise, and that's true consciously: we stop noticing it.
But the body continues to react.
You can sleep in a noisy street and still experience micro-awakenings that degrade the quality of rest.
Health organizations today classify noise among the environmental factors that have a real impact on the health of urban populations.
The main sources are well identified, and road traffic is by far the leading one.

That's why noise reduction measures often align with other policies: reducing speed in the city significantly decreases noise; electric vehicles are quieter at low speeds; some road surfaces absorb sound.
Urban planning also plays a role: distancing housing from major roads, creating quiet zones, protecting the relative silence of parks.
Noise has a disadvantage compared to other pollutants: it is invisible and leaves no trace.
We can't photograph it, we can't measure it at a glance.
Perhaps that's why it has been tolerated for so long.

sentences: There are skills that aren't found in any book, yet they represent a considerable wealth: know-how.
Cutting stone, repairing an old engine, cooking a regional dish, cultivating a local variety, playing a musical repertoire.
These skills have a particularity: they exist in gestures, habits, and accumulated experience.
They are not transmitted just by explaining, but by showing, having others do it, and correcting.
That's what makes them fragile.
Written knowledge can be preserved in a library, even if no one reads it for a century.
Know-how, on the other hand, disappears as soon as a generation stops practicing it.
It exists only as long as it is passed on.
History is full of lost techniques that took a long time to rediscover, or that have never been found again.
Not because they were secret, but because the last person who mastered them died without passing them on.
This transmission is now threatened for several reasons.
The speed of technological changes makes some skills obsolete even before they are transmitted.
The separation of generations reduces opportunities to be around those who know.
And a certain devaluation of manual trades has turned young people away from these learnings.
Efforts exist to preserve these skills: training, apprenticeships, video documentation, recognition of 'masters of art.'
But no recording can completely replace presence.
Many gestures can only be understood by doing them, corrected by someone who has done them a thousand times.
That's why transmission remains a deeply human act, and somewhat urgent.
A piece of know-how that isn't passed on doesn't fade away slowly.
It is lost all at once, with the person who carried it.

sentences: There was a time when leaving your workplace literally meant leaving your job.
You would close the office or workshop door, and what was left to do would wait until the next day.
This boundary, once clear, has gradually faded.
Evening emails, weekend messages, the constant possibility of being reached: work now spills over into spaces and hours that were previously off-limits.
This evolution happened without anyone really deciding it.
The tools that allow remote work were initially presented as a liberation: we could finally organize ourselves as we wished.
But this freedom has turned against us.
Since it’s possible to respond at any moment, it becomes difficult to justify not doing so.
Availability, which was initially optional, has transformed into an implicit expectation.
The consequences, which research is beginning to document, are concerning.
A mind that is never completely disconnected never really rests.
Even without working, one is always on alert.
This underlying vigilance is exhausting, less visibly than a long day, but more enduringly.
Rest assumes that one can, at some point, stop thinking about their obligations — something that constant connectivity makes almost impossible.
Some countries have tried to respond by recognizing a 'right to disconnect' that allows ignoring professional requests outside of working hours.
The intention is good, but a law struggles to change a culture.
As long as availability is seen as proof of commitment, the most conscientious will continue to respond, even if nothing formally obliges them to do so.
Responsibility is therefore shared.
It is up to employers not to reward constant availability and to distinguish real urgency from habit.
But it is also up to everyone to reclaim spaces where work has no place — a meal, an evening, a Sunday.
A life where work never stops is not a more productive life.
It is a life where one no longer rests, and one ultimately loses what only rest can help to rebuild.

sentences: We are promised the 'smart city': a city filled with sensors, capable of continuously measuring traffic, energy consumption, air quality, pedestrian flows, and adjusting its operations accordingly.
Traffic lights that adapt to traffic, lighting that adjusts to presence, optimized transport: the idea is appealing, and its promises of efficiency are not illusory.
Well designed, such a city could waste less and function better.
However, behind this technically appealing vision lies a question that enthusiasm often forgets: a city that measures everything is also a city that monitors everything.
The same sensors that optimize traffic can track people's movements.
The same data that improves a service can be used to control, profile, and predict behaviors.
The line between an efficient city and a surveillance city is thinner than one might think.
We must therefore ask who holds this data and for what purposes.
Too often, the infrastructure of the smart city is designed and operated by private companies, which gain valuable knowledge about the residents.
In exchange for a few conveniences, they find themselves constantly observed, often without having wanted or even understood it.
The city, an ideal common space, risks becoming a vast capture device, to the benefit of a few.
Another concern relates to democracy.
When a city is managed by algorithms, who decides their rules?
Software that allocates resources, directs investments, or prioritizes needs actually wields political power.
Moreover, this power escapes public debate: we do not vote for an algorithm, and we even struggle to understand how it works.
Technical efficiency then tends to replace collective choice.
None of this condemns the idea of a smarter city.
Technology can provide real services, as long as it remains a means and not an end.
But this requires us to ask the right questions from the outset: who controls the data, for what purpose, under what democratic oversight?

sentences: Few institutions have changed as much, in such a short time, as the family.
The model that seemed so obvious just a few decades ago — a married couple for life, surrounded by their children — is now just one form among many.
Blended families, single-parent families, childless families, uniting same-sex couples: the diversity of configurations is now the norm.
In the face of this transformation, a concern arises: are we witnessing the decline, or even the disappearance, of the family?
This fear is based on a misunderstanding.
What is declining is not the family, but a particular form of family, historically situated, that we had come to see as the only possible one.
However, history shows that the family has always varied according to the times and places.
The model we believed to be eternal was itself just a moment in a long evolution.
So, what we are observing is not the end of the family, but a new metamorphosis.
What remains, across all these forms, is the essential function of the family: to provide a lasting bond, a place of belonging, and support in the face of life's challenges.
That this bond takes on new forms does not make it any less real.
A child raised with love by a single parent, or by two same-sex parents, does not lack a family; they simply have one that does not resemble the image of the past.
It would be naive to deny that these changes also pose difficulties.
Blended families must invent bonds without an established model; isolated parents bear a heavy burden alone; the reference points, less obvious, must be constructed rather than received.
Recognizing the richness of these new forms does not mean ignoring the challenges they present.
But the essential point may lie elsewhere.
What makes a family has never been conformity to a model, but the quality of the bonds that unite its members: attention, loyalty, love that withstands the test of time.
In this light, a family that does not resemble any image of the past can be a fully-fledged family, and a family that appears conventional may only have the appearance of one.
The family is not disappearing; it is reinventing itself, as it always has.
And as long as human beings need to be loved and supported by others over time, it will continue to exist, in a thousand forms.

sentences: We spend a considerable part of our childhood and youth at school.
However, if we were asked about what we learned there, many pieces of knowledge would surprisingly be forgotten.
The dates, formulas, and rules that we patiently memorized have mostly vanished.
This somewhat troubling observation leads to a radical question: do we really learn at school, and if so, what exactly?
One might be tempted to conclude that school fails, since so much of its content is forgotten.
But this conclusion is based on a narrow understanding of what learning means.
Reducing education to the accumulation of knowledge misses the essential point.
For what remains, years later, is not the list of accumulated knowledge, but something deeper and more lasting.
What remains, first of all, are ways of thinking.
Learning to read a text, to follow a reasoning, to solve a problem, to doubt a statement: these skills, once acquired, are not forgotten like a date.
They have become incorporated, becoming ways of approaching the world.
We forget the content of a math class; we often retain, without realizing it, the rigor it helped to develop.
What remains next is a relationship to knowledge.
School, when it succeeds, does not just transmit knowledge: it teaches how to learn, awakens curiosity, and shows that one can understand what seemed obscure.
This confidence in one's own ability to grasp the world may be the most precious legacy, as it allows one to continue learning long after leaving the school benches.
What remains, finally, are encounters and openings.

A teacher who has instilled a passion for a subject, a book that has revealed a world, an idea that has transformed a way of seeing: these moments shape a life more surely than a thousand forgotten lessons.
School is not just a place where one accumulates; it is a place where one can be awakened.
Recognizing this does not exempt us from questioning what school transmits and how it does so.
But this shifts the question.
The goal of education is not to fill heads with knowledge destined to fade; it is to form minds capable of thinking, understanding, and continuing to learn.
By this measure, what is forgotten is not what matters most.

sentences: It is often said that we should listen to what people do rather than what they say.
This is especially true when it comes to money.
Our discussions about our values can be misleading, but our spending rarely lies: it often reveals better than our words what we truly value.
Looking at where our money goes is like looking at ourselves in a sometimes surprising mirror.
Everyone willingly states what matters to them: family, health, culture, others.
But does an honest examination of our spending always confirm these statements?
Sometimes we claim to value something while actually dedicating neither money nor time to it, while we spend freely on what we profess to disdain.
This gap between proclaimed values and lived values is mercilessly highlighted by money.
This observation is not a moral judgment; rather, it is a tool for clarity.
Examining our spending is not about feeling guilty, but about getting to know ourselves.
By concretely seeing where our money goes, we discover our actual priorities, those that govern our daily choices, beyond the intentions we display.
And it sometimes happens that this discovery is uncomfortable, as it reveals a gap between the life we lead and the one we wish to lead.
This exercise then opens up a possibility: that of realigning our spending with our values.
If I notice that I spend a lot on what matters little to me, and little on what truly matters, I can correct my course.
Spending consciously does not necessarily mean spending less; it means spending in accordance with what we care about.
A budget, from this perspective, is not an accounting constraint, but the concrete expression of a set of priorities.
We must guard against a trap here: the one that believes everything boils down to money.
Many precious things cannot be bought, and a life is not merely the sum of its expenses.
But in a world where money is the means to so many things, the way we use it remains a faithful indicator of who we are.
Asking myself 'where does my money go?' is therefore indirectly asking 'what really matters to me?'
The answer, inscribed in our statements more surely than in our speeches, deserves to be faced.

sentences: The law is binding, and a society cannot function if everyone decides to obey only the laws that suit them.
This requirement is the foundation of all communal life: without a general respect for the laws, there would be disorder, where the strongest imposes their will.
However, history has seen deeply unjust laws — laws that oppressed, excluded, and allowed inhumane acts.
In the face of such laws, a formidable question arises: should one obey a law deemed unjust?
This dilemma, as old as law itself, does not admit a simple answer.
One position argues that one must always obey the law, whatever it may be, even if it means working peacefully to change it.
The argument is strong: if everyone believed they were allowed to disobey laws they consider unjust, there would be no law at all, since everyone has their own idea of justice.
Disobedience, even if well-intentioned, would open the door to general arbitrariness and the law of the strongest.
It is therefore better to obey while advocating for change, in respect of common rules.
This position has stability and order on its side.
But taken to extremes, it leads to an unsustainable conclusion: one would have to obey the worst laws, participate in the worst injustices, under the pretext that they are legal.
History shows where this absolute obedience leads: to crimes committed 'in the name of the law' by people who hid behind their duty to obey.
If legality justified everything, no law, however monstrous, could ever be disobeyed.
Yet our conscience refuses to accept that the mere fact that something is legal makes it just or obligatory.
A second position thus asserts that there is a justice superior to the law, by virtue of which one can, at times, disobey.
When a law violates the most fundamental requirements of humanity, obeying it becomes a fault, and resisting it, a duty.
It is in the name of such a conviction that men and women have disobeyed unjust laws, often at the cost of their freedom or their lives, and that we honor them today.
Their example shows that obedience is not always a virtue, nor is disobedience always a crime.
The question remains as to when disobedience is legitimate, as it cannot be based solely on our preferences.

A thought has developed around this question, that of civil disobedience, which specifies its conditions: that it concerns a serious injustice and not a mere disagreement; that disobedience is public and not clandestine; that it is non-violent; and that the one who disobeys accepts to bear the legal consequences.
Under these conditions, disobeying is not denying the law, but calling for a better law, in the name of justice.
Should we then obey unjust laws?
As a general rule, yes, because obedience to the laws is the condition of communal life, and disagreement must first seek the path of legal change.
But there is a point beyond which injustice becomes so grave that obedience itself becomes complicity.
Recognizing this point, without abusing it, is one of the heaviest responsibilities of a citizen.
The law deserves respect; justice, even more so — and knowing how to distinguish, in extreme cases, what we owe to each, is perhaps the very mark of conscience.

sentences: For over a century, a promise has recurred with every technical advancement: machines will free us from work.
By taking on the hard tasks for us, they were supposed to offer us unprecedented leisure time, a life finally free from toil.
Some thinkers even predicted that our descendants would only work a few hours a day, mainly occupied with cultivating their minds.
Yet this promised paradise has never quite arrived.
Why does this promise, constantly renewed, always elude us?
We must first acknowledge what the promise has going for it.

Machines have indeed accomplished wonders: they have spared us a huge amount of exhausting work, multiplied what a human being can produce, and made possible a level of comfort that no previous era had known.
In this sense, they have freed us from countless hardships.
No one today would want to return to the exhausting work of the past, and that kind of liberation is real, significant, and achieved.
And yet, the promised free time has not followed in proportion.
Despite gigantic productivity gains, we are not working radically less than we did several decades ago, and many even feel more rushed, more overwhelmed than ever.
How can we explain this paradox?
Where have the hours that machines were supposed to give us gone?
A first answer lies in what we have done with these gains.
Rather than converting them into free time, we have, for the most part, converted them into increased production and consumption.
Machines have allowed us to produce faster; we have chosen to produce more rather than work less.
The time that technology freed up, we immediately filled with new needs, new desires, and a constantly rising standard of living.
Liberation was possible; we preferred abundance instead.
A second answer relates to distribution.
The fruits of automation have not been shared equally: they have mainly benefited some, while others continued to work hard, sometimes even harder.
The free time gained by some has sometimes come at the cost of intensified work for others.
The promise of general liberation assumed a sharing that did not take place, and without which machines free some by enslaving others.
This means that liberation through machines has never been an automatic consequence of technology, but depended on choices we did not make.
Nothing in the machines themselves condemns us to work so much; it is our social organization, our priorities, our race for consumption that determines this.
The promise could still be fulfilled — but it requires a genuine desire for free time rather than endless production growth.
Machines can free us; we just need to decide to do so.

sentences: In the face of the flood of information, often dubious, that comes our way, one might feel disarmed.
How can we untangle the true from the false when we are not specialists ourselves?
The good news is that verifying information does not require inaccessible expertise; it is an art that can be learned, made up of a few simple reflexes that anyone can acquire.
These reflexes do not guarantee infallibility, but they are enough to avoid most of the grossest traps.
The first reflex is to question the source.
Where does this information come from?
Who disseminates it, and what is its reliability?
Serious information generally comes from an identifiable source that takes responsibility and can be held accountable for what it publishes.
Be wary of anonymous sources, unverifiable origins, and websites about which we know nothing: this simple reflex already eliminates many false news stories.
And when several reliable and independent sources confirm information, the trust we can place in it increases.
The second reflex is to distinguish between types of content.
Information is not a comment; a fact is not an opinion; a testimony is not proof.
Many confusions arise from mistaking what is merely an interpretation, a hypothesis, or a position for an established fact.

Learning to identify whether we are dealing with a verifiable fact or an opinion, with raw information or its commentary, is essential to avoid confusing what is demonstrated with what is merely asserted.
The third reflex is to be wary of our own reaction.
As we have seen: what moves us the most is precisely what we should be most cautious about.
Information that provokes a strong emotion in us—indignation, schadenfreude, fear—should trigger not immediate sharing, but a moment of pause.
Asking ourselves 'why do I want to believe this?' is often more useful than asking 'is it true?', because our excitement is the best ally of falsehood.
Doubt should first be directed at what we like too much.
The fourth reflex is to cross-check and trace back to the original source.
Information passed from hand to hand becomes distorted, amplified, and loses its context.

Searching for where it originally came from, what was actually said or found, often reveals that a spectacular news story was based on a misunderstanding, a truncated quote, or an image taken out of context.
This tracing work requires a bit of effort, but it foils many manipulations.
These reflexes do not turn anyone into an infallible expert, and there will always be difficult cases where the true is hard to distinguish from the false.
But they are enough to avoid being the prey of the most common deceptions and to distinguish serious information from unfounded rumors.
Above all, they rely less on knowledge than on an attitude: that of methodical doubt, slowness, and vigilance.
In essence, verifying is refusing to believe too quickly—and this is something anyone can learn.

sentences: We willingly celebrate generosity, the virtue of those who help, give, and dedicate themselves to others.
And this celebration is justified: helping others is one of the most beautiful things a human being can do.
But we talk much less about the other side of this relationship, which is more discreet and often more difficult: that of receiving.
However, accepting help, allowing oneself to be assisted, depending on others, is sometimes more difficult than helping oneself, and this difficulty deserves our attention.
Why is it so hard to receive?
First, because of pride, or what we take for dignity.
Asking for help, admitting that we can't do it alone, showing our weakness, clashes with the desire to be strong, autonomous, and capable.
In a culture that values independence and considers self-sufficiency a virtue, needing others is almost seen as a failure, a decline.
We often prefer to suffer in silence rather than acknowledge that we need help, as if the need itself were shameful.
There is also the fear of debt.
Receiving creates an obligation, an imbalance: the one who has received feels indebted, in a position of inferiority to the one who has given.
This asymmetry is uncomfortable; it can weigh on the relationship, introducing a feeling of dependence or humiliation.
Many refuse help precisely to avoid feeling indebted, to maintain a form of equality or independence.
Receiving means accepting that we are not even, and that comes at a cost.
Yet, knowing how to receive is at least as great a virtue as knowing how to give, and perhaps rarer.
For accepting help is to humbly acknowledge one's own vulnerability, to trust the other, and to accept not being all-powerful.
It is also, paradoxically, a gift to the one who helps: by allowing them to assist us, we offer them the joy of being useful, of giving, of mattering to us.
Refusing all help, in the name of pride, deprives the other of this joy and severs the bond that the received help would have woven.
There is pride in never accepting anything.
This reflection touches on the very nature of community ties.
A community does not only consist of people who give, but of the circulation of help, where everyone takes turns helping and being helped, giving and receiving.
Those who always want to give without ever receiving place themselves above others, in a generosity that may hide a refusal of the bond of equality.
True reciprocity requires that we also accept to receive, to allow ourselves to be helped, to recognize that we need others as much as they need us.
Learning to receive is therefore, in its own way, a lesson in humility and connection.
It is to accept that we are vulnerable, interdependent beings who cannot manage alone and do not have to manage alone.
In a world that exalts autonomy and views need as a weakness, knowing how to ask for and accept help is an act of wisdom and trust.

For a life in which one would never need anyone would not be a more successful life; it would be a poorer life, cut off from what the human bond has of the deepest: the fact that we count on each other.

sentences: The fact that the first question asked of a stranger is about their job says a lot about our era.
We define ourselves, and we define others, by work, to the point of confusing being with doing, the person with their role.
This identification seems so natural that we believe it to be universal.
However, it is a recent historical construction, specific to societies where paid work has become central to existence, and there is no guarantee that it will last.
Questioning it does not deny the importance of work, but rather rejects the idea that it should absorb our entire identity.
We must first assess what is particular about this identification.
In many societies, past or present, people primarily define themselves by their lineage, community, faith, or status, not by productive activity.
Work there is what one does to live, not what defines who one is.

The fact that a job has become, for us, the default answer to the question 'who are you?' stems from a specific history: that of the rise of a society where production has become the cardinal value, and work, the main path to social recognition.
This identification is not inherent; it is dated, situated, and therefore reversible.
It certainly has its virtues.
Work structures existence, integrates individuals into a collective, and provides a sense of being useful and recognized.
Identifying with one's job also means valuing what one does, investing pride in it, and finding a part of meaning there.

It would be somewhat hypocritical to disdain this identification from the comfort of a leisurely life: for many, work is what gives their days shape and dignity, and depriving it of its identity dimension would impoverish them.
Critiquing identity through work should not slip into disdain for work itself.
But this identification has a downside, which becomes apparent when it becomes exclusive.
If I am only my job, who am I when I lose it — due to unemployment, illness, or retirement?

The experience of those who are left by work reveals the fragility of an identity that has no other foundation: it wavers, empties, as if what has been taken from the person is not just a job, but a part of themselves.

A society that has taught its members to exist only through their function leaves them helpless as soon as that function eludes them, and prepares, as work becomes scarcer or transforms, a crisis of identity as much as of employment.
There is more.
Identification with work also serves a logic that is not innocent.

By making work the primary place of value and recognition, a society directs energies towards production, subordinates other dimensions of existence to professional activity, and casts suspicion on any life that would not be defined by work.
Those who do not produce — whether because they cannot or do not want to — are denied a part of their dignity, as if they were failing a duty to exist usefully.
This pressure, internalized, transforms work from a means into an end, and the human being into a producer who exists only as they produce.
Recognizing the constructed nature of identity through work gives us the freedom to relativize it.
Not to devalue work, which retains its importance, but to assign it its rightful place: a dimension of existence among others, not the entirety of it.
A human being is also a relative, a citizen, a curious person, a creator, a living being — roles that no job description records.

Remembering that we are not reducible to what we do to earn a living preserves, against an era that tends to forget it, a broader conception of what a person is — and allows us to maintain, for the day when work might be lacking, a foundation of identity that its loss could not take away.

sentences: There is a way of speaking that has turned the absence of content into an art: jargon.

It is recognized by its ability to produce a lot of words without saying anything, stringing together hollow phrases, chaining obvious statements and generalities that commit to nothing and cannot be contradicted because they mean almost nothing.
This language, long associated with authoritarian regimes and their propaganda, has spread far beyond that, permeating ordinary political, managerial, and institutional discourse.
It deserves to be examined, as its success reveals a precise and formidable function.
Jargon is primarily characterized by vagueness.
It prefers vague words to precise terms, abstractions to concrete realities, and ready-made phrases to verifiable statements.

People talk about 'dynamics,' 'synergies,' 'implementation of measures,' and 'supporting transitions' — expressions that give the impression of saying something while avoiding any claims that could be discussed or denied.
This vagueness is not a clumsiness; it serves a purpose.
It allows one to speak without committing, to occupy space without taking risks, to seem to respond without actually responding.
For this is the first utility of jargon: to avoid compromising oneself.
Saying something precise exposes one — to contradiction, reproach, and verification.
Jargon, by remaining vague, escapes these risks.
You cannot catch out someone who has said nothing verifiable; you cannot reproach someone for a failure when they have made no precise promises.
This language is an armor: it protects the user from any accountability, at the cost of a void that it masks with an abundance of words.
Its second utility is to anesthetize.
Jargon dulls vigilance; through expected phrases and conventional turns of speech, it creates a sort of humming that discourages attention.
People stop truly listening, let these words slide by without grabbing anything, and give up searching for a meaning that they do not have.
In doing so, it disarms critical thinking: one does not contest a discourse that one no longer listens to, one does not get indignant about what one has not grasped.
Jargon conveys, under the guise of harmless verbiage, the absence of any real content — and sometimes, the evasion of what one does not want to say.
One must be careful here to avoid confusion.
Not all caution in language is jargon; there are delicate subjects where nuance and restraint are legitimate, where one must weigh their words.
Jargon is distinguished from this honest caution by its intention: it does not weigh its words to say something accurate, but empties them to say nothing.
Caution seeks accuracy; jargon seeks to evade.
One refines thought, the other dissolves it.
Knowing how to distinguish them is necessary to avoid confusing rigor with emptiness.
Resisting jargon requires a demand: to ask, behind the words, what is actually being said.
What does this phrase concretely mean?
What does it assert that could be true or false?
What does it commit to?
These questions, directed at any discourse, reveal the void where it exists and sometimes force those who speak to emerge from their verbal armor.

In a democracy, this demand is a civic duty, for jargon is not just a laziness of language: it is a way of governing without accountability, of speaking to avoid being understood, of drowning under words what should be clearly stated and openly debated.

sentences: Mass culture — this vast array of productions intended for the greatest number, disseminated on an industrial scale, from series to popular songs, from blockbusters to games — has long sparked a debate between two irreconcilable positions.
For some, it represents a degradation, a decline of culture, an easy entertainment that dulls the masses and stifles true creation.
For others, it is a happy democratization, finally granting access to a culture that was long reserved for an elite.
These two equally assured positions deserve to be transcended, as each captures a part of the truth while veering into excess.
The elitist critique of mass culture is not without foundation.
It is true that a significant portion of mass production follows a commercial logic that prioritizes what immediately pleases the greatest number, to the detriment of rigor, difficulty, and novelty.
It is also true that this logic tends to standardize, reproduce tried-and-true formulas, and flatter established tastes rather than elevate them.
Finally, it is true that entertainment designed to occupy without effort can dull critical thinking, divert attention from more demanding creations, and foster a habit of ease.
These critiques touch on something real, and dismissing them in the name of democracy would be blind.
But the elitist critique, taken to extremes, falls into a contempt that disqualifies it.
For it looks down on the tastes and pleasures of the vast majority, deeming them vulgar simply because they are shared.
It assumes that what pleases the majority is thereby worthless, and that true culture is the privilege of a few distinguished minds.
This stance, besides its arrogance, is false: popular culture has produced works of real value, and the fact that a work pleases many does not prove it is mediocre.
Confusing rigor with rarity, deeming everything that is shared as vulgar, turns culture into an instrument of social distinction rather than a good to be shared.
The opposite position, which unreservedly celebrates mass culture in the name of democracy, also has its share of truth and its excess.

Its truth: mass dissemination has indeed granted access to culture for populations that were previously excluded, broken the monopoly of elites, and allowed everyone to enjoy works and pleasures once reserved for a select few.
This is a real progress, and lamenting it would be a guilty nostalgia for a time when culture was a privilege.
Its excess: rejecting any hierarchy, considering all productions as equivalent, and making popularity the sole criterion of value.
For while success does not prove mediocrity, it does not prove excellence either; the number of people who love a work does not measure its value.
Moving beyond this false debate requires rejecting the alternative between elitist disdain and populist complacency.
One can acknowledge that mass culture has democratized access to culture, which is a good thing, and that it often follows a logic that impoverishes, which is a risk.
One can appreciate popular works without renouncing rigor, distinguishing within mass production what has value from what does not, without looking down on the people or flattering all their tastes.
The real question is not "Is mass culture good or bad?", but "How can we ensure that a culture accessible to all remains a demanding culture?".
For the real issue lies here: not choosing between the elite and the masses, between rigor and accessibility, but refusing to oppose them.
A culture that is demanding but reserved for a few would betray its vocation to be shared; a culture that is accessible but renounces all rigor would betray its vocation to elevate.
The ideal would be a culture that is both demanding and shared, which sacrifices neither quality for dissemination nor dissemination for quality.

This ideal is difficult, never fully achieved, but it is toward this that we must strive — rather than resigning ourselves to the false choice between a quality culture for a few and a degraded culture for all.

sentences: Few things seem as natural as passing on to one's children what one has acquired.
Working for one's family, leaving them an inheritance, ensuring their future: this aspiration seems so obvious that we hesitate to question it.
And yet, inheritance harbors a deep contradiction with another principle we cherish, that of equal opportunity.
For what inheritance transmits is not just material goods: it conveys unearned advantages that mean children do not start life on equal footing.
This tension deserves to be confronted, however uncomfortable it may be.
The principle of equal opportunity holds that success should depend on merit, effort, personal qualities, and not on the circumstances of one's birth.
However, inheritance directly contradicts this principle.
A child who inherits a fortune, a legacy, or a network has considerable advantages that they have not earned, which are due to nothing but the chance of being born into a certain family.
Two children of equal worth, one born rich and the other poor, will not have the same chances, and this difference is entirely due to inheritance.
Thus, it perpetuates, from generation to generation, inequalities that are not justified from the standpoint of merit.

One might argue that someone who has acquired an asset has the right to dispose of it as they see fit, including passing it on to their children; prohibiting inheritance would be an infringement on freedom and property.
This argument has its strength, but it faces a difficulty: the right of the giver conflicts with the right of all other children to equal opportunity.
The freedom to bequeath creates the starting inequality for others.

It is not obvious that the first right should absolutely take precedence over the second; one could argue that society has a legitimate interest in limiting the transmission of privileges to preserve a certain equality of opportunity among newcomers.
There is something even more troubling.
Inheritance does not only transmit material goods, but a whole set of more subtle and determining advantages: education, culture, manners, relationships, codes, aspirations.
These advantages, even more than wealth, are transmitted and perpetuated, reproducing social positions from generation to generation.
Even if we were to abolish material inheritance, these immaterial inheritances would continue to deepen the inequality of opportunity.
Inheritance, in the broad sense, is the mechanism by which a society reproduces its hierarchies, ensuring that children essentially inherit their parents' position.
Should we conclude that inheritance should be abolished?
The question is more complex than what the stark positions suggest.

On one hand, unlimited inheritance perpetuates unjust inequalities and contradicts equal opportunity; on the other hand, completely prohibiting it would be both unrealistic, infringing on legitimate attachments, and powerless to eliminate the immaterial inheritances that weigh the most.

Between unlimited inheritance and its abolition, there are intermediate positions: regulating, taxing, limiting the transmission of large fortunes, while preserving ordinary inheritance; investing in education to compensate for immaterial inheritances.
These measures do not eliminate the tension, but they do mitigate it.
The essential point may be not to sweep the contradiction under the false evidence of 'it's natural.'

Recognizing that inheritance, however understandable it may be, contradicts equal opportunity, and that what we pass on to our children unfairly advantages some at the expense of others, is to refuse to accept as just what is merely customary.
One can, with full knowledge, choose to maintain a part of inheritance, weighing the values at stake; but one should not do so while pretending that there is no problem.

For behind the apparent obviousness of passing on to one's own lies one of the most powerful mechanisms for perpetuating inequalities — and confronting it is the condition for any honest judgment on the justice of our societies.

sentences: We want two things that seem to contradict each other: to stay ourselves and to be able to change.
On one hand, we value continuity, being the same person over time, and we are wary of those who "change completely" like a traitor to themselves.
On the other hand, we aspire to evolve, to correct ourselves, to become better, and a life without change would seem like stagnation to us.
How can we reconcile these two demands?
Can we change profoundly while still being ourselves, or does changing necessarily mean ceasing to be who we were?
This question, which concludes our reflection on identity, brings together its threads.
The contradiction is only apparent if we conceive of identity as something fixed, an immutable core that must be preserved intact.
In this view, indeed, changing would be betrayal, altering that essence which should remain the same.
But we have seen that identity may not be a fixed thing, but rather a story, a process, a dynamic continuity.

Now, a story, precisely, is characterized by the fact that it changes while remaining the same story: the narrative of a life incorporates transformations, evolutions, even breaks, without ceasing to be the narrative of a single life.
Change is not the opposite of identity; it is its very movement, provided it is inscribed within a continuity.
For what makes the continuity of an identity through change is not the absence of change, but the way in which changes are linked and integrated.
I remain myself not because I do not change, but because my changes are my own, stemming from my history, connecting to it, even extending it while transforming it.
The child I was, the adult I am, the old person I will be, differ profoundly, and yet a continuity connects them: that of a story that continues, where each stage arises from the previous one.
Changing without betraying oneself means changing within the continuity of one's story, not through arbitrary breaks that would shatter it.
This conception allows us to distinguish two kinds of changes.

There is the change that extends and fulfills, where one becomes more oneself by evolving, where the transformation realizes a continuity rather than breaking it: such is the case for one who matures, deepens, corrects their mistakes while remaining recognizable in what they become.
And there is the change that betrays, where one renounces what they were, where one breaks with their values, where the transformation is a renunciation rather than an accomplishment.
The difference does not lie in the magnitude of the change, but in its relation to continuity: the first is inscribed in a story and continues it, the second breaks it.
Moreover, there are profound changes that, far from betraying, are required by fidelity to oneself.
The one who recognizes their mistake and corrects it, who abandons an untenable conviction, who transforms to remain true to what they hold as true, changes out of fidelity, not betrayal.

True fidelity to oneself is not immobility, the refusal of all change; it is sometimes the ability to change to remain faithful to the essential, to transform what one is in order not to betray what one believes.
Stubbornness in error out of fear of changing would be false fidelity; changing to be more just can be the true fidelity.
Changing without betraying oneself is therefore not only possible but necessary for a vibrant life.
An identity that would refuse all change would freeze, dry up, and cease to be alive; an identity that would change without continuity would dissolve and be lost.

Between stagnation that refuses to evolve and dissolution that loses all thread, there is the path of a living identity: one that changes while remaining faithful to its story, that evolves without renouncing itself, that becomes other while remaining itself.
Ultimately, being oneself does not mean staying identical; it means remaining the coherent author of a story that, to stay alive, never ceases to transform.

sentences: Among the many differences that separate France and Great Britain, the relationship to rules is one of the most revealing, as it touches on deep conceptions of freedom, authority, and social order.
It is often summarized by images: the Briton who queues with discipline, the Frenchman who contests and circumvents.

These images, necessarily simplified, do capture a real difference that deserves to be analyzed beyond the cliché, as it sheds light on two ways of conceiving the link between the individual and the common rule.
The British relationship to rules is based on a fundamental trust.

Rules are generally perceived as legitimate, useful, and an expression of a tacit pact that benefits everyone; respecting them is not submission, but participation in an order that one recognizes as their own.

This trust has historical roots: a political evolution that occurred through progressive reforms rather than breaks, which preserved the continuity of institutions and fostered the feeling that rules emanated from an order to which one adhered.
Respect for rules goes hand in hand with a certain sense of fair play: everyone plays the game because they trust that others will do so as well, and that the game, overall, is fair.
The French relationship to rules is more distrustful, more critical.

Rules are spontaneously suspected, judged, and required to justify themselves; they are not respected by principle, but to the extent that they are recognized as founded, and one reserves the right to contest, circumvent, or even oppose them if deemed unjust.

This disposition also has historical roots: a political history made up of breaks and revolutions, where contesting established authority has been elevated to a founding virtue; a tradition that sees critical spirit and resistance to arbitrariness as cardinal values.
Contesting the rule is not seen as incivility, but often as an affirmation of one's freedom and judgment.
These two relationships stem from two conceptions of freedom.

For the British sensibility, freedom accommodates the respect for rules, provided they are just and accepted; obeying a rule that one recognizes as legitimate does not alienate in any way, and order is the condition for everyone's freedom.

For the French sensibility, freedom implies the permanent right to judge the rule, not to submit to it blindly, and to resist what one deems unjust; obedience without examination seems suspect, as an abdication of judgment.
One sees in the rule a pact that protects freedom; the other sees a power that must be treated with caution.
Each of these relationships has its virtues and vices, and one illuminates the other by contrast.

The British respect for rules produces an orderly, fluid, courteous society, where communal life unfolds with remarkable civility; but it can lead to a docility that accepts rules that deserve to be contested, and a conformism that confuses order with justice.

The French critical spirit maintains a salutary vigilance against arbitrariness, a capacity to resist injustice; but it can degenerate into chronic indiscipline, systematic contestation, and difficulty in agreeing on common rules and enforcing them.
Understanding these two relationships means understanding that neither holds the truth, but that each reveals the limits of the other.
The Briton would sometimes benefit from contesting more, the Frenchman from respecting more; one could learn from the other's critical vigilance, the other from their civic trust.
Neither disposition is superior in itself: they respond differently to the same tension between the order that makes communal life possible and the freedom that refuses to submit to it blindly.

Observing them in relation to each other allows us to realize that our own relationship to rules, which we believe to be natural, is actually a choice among other possibilities — and to discover, in the neighbor's mirror, what our own assumptions have of particular.

sentences: Abundance societies have realized a millennia-old dream of humanity: they have largely conquered scarcity, providing their members with a profusion of goods, leisure, and opportunities that past generations would not have dared to dream of.
One might expect this abundance to bring happiness in proportion to it.
However, a paradox emerges: within this very profusion, a feeling of emptiness, dissatisfaction, and sometimes depression spreads.
Why is it that abundance, far from filling, often seems to deepen a void?
This question strikes at the heart of the malaise in wealthy societies.
A first explanation lies in the mechanism of habituation and desire.
We quickly get used to what we possess; the long-desired good, once obtained, rapidly ceases to bring us joy, and a new desire takes its place.
Abundance, by satisfying our desires, does not therefore soothe desire itself, which shifts and renews endlessly.
We get what we want, and immediately we want something else; satisfaction is brief, and lack is perpetual.
Abundance does not fill desire; it sustains it, keeping us in a state of dissatisfaction that no good can satisfy.
The more we have, the more we want, and the void deepens as our possessions increase.
A second explanation relates to the nature of what abundance provides.
It offers us material goods, pleasures, and entertainment; but these things do not fulfill the deepest need of human beings, which is a need for meaning, relationships, and fulfillment.
Material abundance can coexist with a poverty of meaning; one can have everything that can be bought and lack what cannot be purchased.

The emptiness within abundance may be that of a need that abundance cannot fulfill, because it pertains to something else: it fills our lives with goods, but not with meaning, and it is meaning that we hunger for.
There is something more troubling.
Abundance itself can generate a particular form of emptiness, due to the excess of choices it offers.
Faced with a profusion of possibilities, we are paralyzed, unable to choose, dissatisfied with our choices that deprive us of all others, haunted by what we could have had.
The abundance of possibilities, far from liberating, can overwhelm; too many choices lead to indecision, regret, and dissatisfaction.
We have so many options that we no longer know how to want them, so many possibilities that we do not fully realize any of them, scattered in a field of possibilities where we fixate on nothing.
The abundance of possibilities is also a dispersion, where emptiness arises from excess.
This diagnosis does not lead to praising scarcity, nor to regretting material poverty, which has been and remains a very real misfortune.
The emptiness of abundance is a problem of the rich, and it would be indecent to compare it to the distress of lack.

But it reveals an important truth: that the satisfaction of material needs, however necessary it may be, is not enough for happiness, and that a civilization that has conquered scarcity without addressing the need for meaning would not have conquered unhappiness.
Abundance solves one problem — that of material lack — without resolving the one that persists beyond: the need for meaning, relationships, and fulfillment, which no profusion of goods can satisfy.
Thus, escaping the emptiness of abundance does not mean renouncing it, but understanding what it cannot give, and seeking it elsewhere.

It is to recognize that meaning cannot be bought, that deep relationships cannot be consumed, that fulfillment is not found in possession; it is to stop expecting from material abundance what it cannot provide, in order to invest in what alone fulfills the deepest need.
It may also be about learning to desire differently, to step out of the race for possession that sustains lack, to find in sufficiency what excess does not provide.

The emptiness of abundance is not a fatality; it is a sign that we are looking in the wrong place for what abundance does not contain — and that we must, even within the profusion, relearn where to find what truly fulfills.

sentences: Every morning, around ten o'clock, the postman comes down my street.
His name is Marc.
He has a yellow bike and a big bag of letters.
Marc knows everyone.
He knows the names, the houses, the dogs.
He says hello to everyone, even when it rains.
"The postman is the neighborhood's newspaper," says my grandmother.
That's true.
Marc knows everything: the new baby, the new neighbors, the lost and found cat.
As for me, I mostly receive advertisements.
Pizzas, supermarkets.
Sometimes, a bill.
I throw away almost everything.
But this morning, it's different.
Marc rings my doorbell.
"A letter for you!
A real one!" he says, happy.
A real letter, with a stamp.
I recognize the handwriting: it's my cousin Emma, in Canada.
I open the letter with a coffee.
Emma talks about her new life, her job, the snow.
She writes: "Write back to me with a real letter."
This afternoon, I buy some paper and a stamp.
A real letter feels good.
Thank you, Emma.
And thank you, Marc.
