sentences: At the end of these reflections on time, memory, and identity, one question remains, the most existential of all: how do we live with the passage of time?

For everything we have said comes down to this observation: time passes, taking everything with it—our days, our joys, our loved ones, ourselves; and this passage is the source of our deepest anxieties.
In the face of it, two opposing temptations arise, both equally futile; and perhaps there is a third way, more difficult but wiser, where a form of peace could be found.
The first temptation is to want to hold on to what passes, to fight against the passage of time, to try to stop the moment, to preserve what is leaving.
This temptation is deeply human: we would like to freeze the happy moment, keep what we love, prevent time from tearing away what is dear to us.
But this struggle is doomed from the start, and wanting to hold on to what passes is to condemn oneself to the suffering of perpetual failure.
We cannot hold back time; it slips away regardless of what we do, and clinging to what is leaving, refusing its passage, only adds the pain of futile resistance to the inevitable loss.

He who wants to hold on to the moment misses it, for he does not live it, so preoccupied is he with wanting to fix it; and he suffers doubly, from the passage he cannot prevent and from his own powerlessness.
The second, opposite temptation is to resign oneself to the passage of time, to detach oneself from it, to give up on attaching to what will pass anyway.
Since everything goes away, why bother to attach?
It would be better not to love too much, not to hold anything as precious, to protect oneself against loss by refusing attachment.
This wisdom of detachment, advocated by certain traditions, has its nobility and coherence; but it also has its price, which is to deprive oneself of life itself.
For not attaching to anything to avoid losing anything is to renounce love, enjoyment, and living fully; it is to protect oneself from the pain of loss at the cost of the richness of attachment.
Total detachment avoids suffering, but it also avoids life; it buys peace at the price of emptiness.
Between these two temptations—holding on to what passes or detaching from it—there may be a third way, more difficult, where a form of wisdom could be found.

It would consist of loving what passes not despite its passage, but in a sense because of it; savoring the moment precisely because it is unique and will not return; cherishing what is dear to us knowing that we will lose it, and loving all the more intensely because we know the loss is inevitable.

This way does not deny the passage of time, as the first temptation does; it does not protect itself from it through detachment, as the second does; it accepts it, and makes it the very source of the value of what passes.
For it is because the moment flees that it is precious; it is because we die that life has value; it is because nothing lasts that everything deserves to be fully lived.
This wisdom is difficult, for it requires holding together what seems contradictory: attachment and consent to loss, love of what passes and acceptance of its flight.

It does not eliminate the pain of losing—this pain is the price of attachment, and refusing it would be to refuse to love—but it transforms our relationship to loss, making finitude not the enemy of value, but its condition.

Loving a being knowing that we will lose it, savoring a moment knowing that it is fleeting, is not to condemn oneself to suffering; it is to love and savor fully, with that intensity that only the awareness of finitude can provide.
The passing time, in this perspective, is no longer just what tears away what we love; it is what gives what we love its irreplaceable value.
Holding on to what passes is impossible; detaching from it is impoverishing; what remains is to love it because it passes.

This is perhaps the highest wisdom regarding time: not the futile struggle against its passage, nor the detachment that deprives us of life, but a lucid and loving consent to finitude, which makes the passage of time not a curse, but the very source of the value and beauty of what is given to us.
Time takes everything from us; but it is also what, by making everything ephemeral, makes everything precious.

Consenting to this, loving fully what we know we must lose, living each moment as unique because it is, is perhaps the only possible victory over time: not to stop it, which is impossible, but to inhabit it so fully that its very passage becomes a reason to love.

sentences: Technical progress has given humanity unprecedented powers: we can transform nature, extend life, communicate instantly across the world, and also destroy on a scale once unimaginable.
These powers are constantly growing, and nothing seems to be able to limit them.
But a question arises, all the more pressing as these powers increase: does our wisdom keep pace with our powers?
Have we become, as our power has grown, wiser and more capable of using what we can do wisely?
And if that is not the case, if our powers are growing faster than our wisdom, what do we risk?
The observation is hard to refute: our technical powers have grown tremendously, but nothing indicates that our wisdom has progressed proportionately.
We are not evidently wiser, fairer, or more in control of our passions than people of the past; we have infinitely more powerful means, but we use them for purposes that are no wiser.
This is a formidable imbalance: for increased power in hands that are not wiser is more dangerous, not less, than lesser power.
The more powerful our means are, the graver our faults can be, and the more catastrophic the consequences of our lack of wisdom can be.
The imbalance between our powers and our wisdom may be the major peril of our time.
This imbalance is strikingly evident in our capacity for destruction.
Humanity has, for the first time in its history, acquired the power to destroy itself, to make the planet uninhabitable, to annihilate civilization.
This terrifying power is in the hands of a humanity that is no wiser than before, still subject to the same passions, the same blind spots, the same follies.
The fact that this unparalleled power of destruction is held by a humanity whose wisdom has not grown proportionately should fill us with concern.
We have the means to destroy ourselves, without having acquired the wisdom that would surely protect us from it.
This imbalance is also evident in our relationship with nature.

Our technical powers have given us an unprecedented ability to transform our environment, but we use it without the wisdom that would measure the consequences, preserve the balances, and safeguard the future.
We are transforming the world on a scale that exceeds our ability to foresee and control the effects, with a power that surpasses our wisdom.

The result is the ecological crisis, which may be the most visible manifestation of the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom: we can transform the planet, but we are not wise enough to do so without destroying it.
Should we conclude that we need to limit technological progress, renouncing powers that our wisdom cannot control?
This conclusion, appealing as it is, is difficult to implement, because no one can stop technological progress, and wanting to do so would be futile.
The real answer may lie elsewhere: not in the illusory limitation of powers, but in the development of wisdom, so that it catches up with our powers.
If our powers grow faster than our wisdom, the solution is not to restrain the powers, but to increase wisdom, ensuring that it grows in proportion to our strength.

This is an immense challenge, as wisdom does not progress like technology, does not accumulate, and must be reclaimed by each generation; but it is the only one that can address the imbalance that threatens us.
This challenge gives a new meaning to what we have said about wisdom, virtue, and self-formation.
For if the major peril of our time is the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom, then the development of wisdom—both individual and collective—is not a luxury, but a vital necessity.

Cultivating wisdom, prudence, self-control, a sense of limits, and responsibility towards the future is not just a matter of personal improvement; it may be the very condition for the survival of humanity, whose powers have exceeded control.

Technological progress, without progress in wisdom, leads to catastrophe; and the great challenge of our time may be to ensure that our wisdom finally catches up with our powers, before the imbalance becomes fatal.
Never has the ancient demand for wisdom been as urgent as in an age where our powers have become excessive.

sentences: Death concerns us not only as our own, to come; it also affects us, and perhaps more painfully, as that of the beings we love.
Losing a loved one is one of the hardest trials of existence, and the question of how to live after this loss, how to go through grief, is one of the most difficult there is.
For grief places us before an apparent dilemma: between forgetting, which seems to betray the one we've lost, and perpetual pain, which freezes us in the loss and prevents us from living.
How can we be faithful to the one we've lost without allowing grief to destroy us?
Grief is primarily a pain, and it would be indecent to want to eliminate it, to pretend to free oneself from it too quickly.
The loss of a loved one is a real tearing; the pain of grief is legitimate, even necessary, as it measures the love we had.
Wanting to escape grief too quickly, rushing to 'turn the page,' would be a way of betraying the one we've lost, denying the importance they had.
Grief requires its time, its work, its pain; we must not rush it, nor be ashamed to suffer, nor let ourselves be pressured to heal.
The pain of grief is the first tribute to the one we've lost.
But grief cannot also be frozen in perpetual pain, in a sorrow that would trap us forever in loss.

Staying indefinitely in pain, refusing to live after the loss, allowing oneself to be destroyed by sorrow, is not honoring the one we lost either; it is letting oneself die with them, refusing the life they would have wanted for us.
There comes a moment when grief, if it does not transform, becomes a prison, a misunderstood fidelity that freezes us in death instead of returning us to life.
Remaining forever in pain is no more faithful than forgetting; it is another way of failing to honor what we owe to the one we lost, and to the life that continues.
How can we escape this dilemma between the betrayal of forgetting and the paralysis of pain?
Perhaps by understanding that true fidelity to the deceased is neither forgetting nor perpetual pain, but the transformation of the bond.

The work of mourning is not to forget the one we lost, nor to remain frozen in sorrow, but to transform our relationship with them: from a lost presence, whose absence tears us apart, to an inner presence, a living memory that accompanies us.
The one we lost does not completely disappear; they remain within us, in what they gave us, in what we learned from them, in the way they continue to inspire us.
Fidelity to the deceased means keeping them alive within us, not as a wound that never heals, but as a presence that nourishes, accompanies, and inspires.
This transformation of the bond allows us to reconcile fidelity and life.
For keeping alive within us the one we have lost, making their memory live on, allowing their influence to continue to guide us, is not to forget them; it is to remain faithful to them.
And this fidelity, far from freezing us in pain, brings us back to life, as it transforms loss into legacy, absence into inner presence, and sorrow into living memory.
We can live after loss, regain joy, look towards the future, all while remaining faithful to the one we have lost, by keeping them alive within us.
True fidelity is not about refusing to live, but about living while carrying within us the one we have lost, making fruitful what they have given us.
Grief, understood this way, is not a choice between forgetting and pain, but a work of transformation, which moves from lost presence to inner presence, from heartbreaking absence to living memory.
This work is long, painful, never quite finished; but it allows us to reconcile fidelity to the deceased and a return to life, to honor the one we have lost without being destroyed by their absence.

And it reveals a truth about love and death: that death separates, but does not entirely destroy the bond; that those we have loved continue to live within us, in what they have given us; and that fidelity to the dead is not about dying with them, but about keeping them alive within us while we ourselves live.

Loving those who are no longer here means carrying them within us, not as a weight that crushes, but as a presence that accompanies — and this may be the highest way to conquer, if not death, at least its power to destroy what love once was.

sentences: Indeed, Mr. Hobson, the traveler replied, is there a mode of transportation more pleasant than ours?
We don't feel like we're moving.
Our island has precisely the same speed as that of the current that carries it away.
Isn't it the same phenomenon that accompanies a balloon in the air?
And what a charm it would be to travel like this with your house, your garden, your park, your very country!
A wandering island, but I mean a real island, with a solid, unsinkable base, would truly be the most comfortable and wonderful vehicle one could imagine.
They say hanging gardens have been made?
Why, one day, wouldn't we create floating parks that would transport us to all corners of the world?
Their size would make them completely insensitive to the waves.
They would have nothing to fear from storms.
Perhaps even, with favorable winds, we could steer them with large sails stretched to the breeze?
And then, what miraculous vegetation would surprise the eyes of the passengers when they passed from temperate zones to tropical zones!
I even imagine that with skilled pilots, well-trained in the currents, we could maintain ourselves under chosen latitudes and enjoy an eternal spring at will!

sentences: One evening, my daughter's hamster, Nono, managed to escape from its cage.
My daughter came to see me, in tears.
"Dad, Nono has disappeared!
The cage is open!"
We searched everywhere in her room: under the bed, behind the wardrobe, in the drawers.
After an hour, still no sign of Nono.
The whole family started to search.
We moved the furniture in the living room, thinking it might have hidden there.
Around eleven o'clock, my husband heard a small noise coming from the kitchen.
We found Nono behind the refrigerator, eating a crumb of bread that had fallen on the floor.
My daughter was so relieved that she cried tears of joy this time.
Since this adventure, we check twice that the cage is properly closed before going to sleep.
Nono doesn't seem to remember anything.
He keeps running on his wheel as if nothing happened.

sentences: A new tramway opened in my city last month, after four years of construction.
The new line connects the city center to the northern suburbs, over a distance of fifteen kilometers.
On the first day, thousands of residents came to try the tramway, for free all weekend.
Many were curious to see what had changed on their street for so long.
Finally, no need to take the car to go to work, said a resident interviewed by a local newspaper.
But not everything went perfectly.
During the first weeks, several breakdowns delayed the users.
The town hall apologized and promised to quickly improve the service.
Some shopkeepers in the city center are also complaining: the construction closed their street for four years, and many customers went elsewhere.
Others, on the contrary, hope that the tramway will attract new customers in the coming months.
The town hall claims that the number of cars in the city center has already started to decrease.
In a year, a second line is expected to open towards the east of the city.

sentences: After five years of study, I graduated last month.
The graduation ceremony took place in a large amphitheater, in front of all the families.
When my name was called, I felt immense pride, thinking about all those years of work.
My parents were in the audience, and I saw my mother wipe away a tear when I went up on stage.
After the ceremony, I met up with my classmates for one last photo together.
We knew that this photo also marked a separation: each of us would now go our own way, towards a new job or a new city.
On my way home that night, I felt a strange mix of joy and sadness.
These five years had been difficult, but they had also been among the richest of my life.
Now, I need to find a job, in a job market that is not always easy for young graduates.
I still don't know exactly what the future holds for me.
But I leave with a diploma, precious friends, and the belief that I made good use of these years.

sentences: On my account, you can see successful vacations, nice meals, and smiles.
You don't see the arguments with my partner, the overdue bills, or the days when I stay in bed longer than I should.
It's not that I'm deliberately lying about my life.
Simply, no one posts a picture of their messy kitchen or their Monday morning fatigue.
The problem is that this natural selection, made by millions of people at the same time, creates a slightly false collective image of reality.
I know this intellectually.
Yet, while looking at others' posts, I sometimes forget this obvious truth, and I compare myself to an idealized version of their life, which I know is partial.
A friend recently confided in me that she was going through a very difficult time, even though her posts during the same weeks showed an apparently serene life.
This confession reminded me of a simple thing: no one shares their entire life online, only the moments they choose to share.
Curiously, I sometimes find myself being more honest about a specific topic with strangers I meet online than with my own followers about my general daily life.
The relative anonymity of these occasional exchanges may take away some of the pressure I feel on my main profile, where I know that close ones are reading me.
I continue to post, too, mainly my good moments.
But I now try to remember that this is also true for everyone around me.

sentences: For several years, I have been sorting my waste, reducing my plastic consumption, and trying to limit food waste.
Despite these efforts, a question regularly crosses my mind: do these small individual actions really have a significant impact, given the immense scale of environmental issues?
Some environmental experts indeed point out that the majority of polluting emissions come from large industries and global political choices, much more than from individual consumption habits.

From this perspective, focusing solely on our personal small actions could almost distract attention from the true culprits, giving a false impression of individual control over a problem that is essentially collective and structural.

Other experts, however, advocate a complementary view: individual habits, when multiplied among millions of people, ultimately end up influencing the companies themselves, pushing them to adapt their offerings in response to a more demanding consumer base.

Talking openly about it around me, without presenting it as a miracle solution, often encourages others to adopt the same habits — a modest but real ripple effect, difficult to measure statistically, that I nonetheless observe very concretely in my close circle.
For my part, I continue to believe in the usefulness of my daily actions, without deluding myself about their individual impact.

I simply think that acting on my scale, while also supporting broader political and industrial changes, remains the most coherent position, rather than passively waiting for others to solve a problem that concerns us all.

sentences: It is often said that a major international sporting competition has the power to unite an entire country, beyond its usual divisions.
For a few weeks, strangers gather in front of the same screen, sharing the same joy or disappointment, seeming to forget, for the duration of a match, their deepest political or social disagreements.
This appealing image, however, deserves to be examined closely.

Is the unity produced by sport really sustainable, or is it merely an emotional interlude that closes as soon as the competition is over, leaving no concrete trace on the real tensions that run through a society?
Several historical examples suggest that this unity, very real in the moment, often remains superficial and temporary.

Countries that have experienced moments of collective joy around a major sporting victory have seen, a few months later, their internal divisions resurface intact, as if this interlude had changed nothing about the underlying causes of these tensions.
Other analyses, however, qualify this pessimistic observation.

Some sociology researchers emphasize that these collective moments, even if fleeting, are not without value: they create a shared experience, a common memory that very different citizens can refer back to later, which contributes, modestly but genuinely, to a form of shared national sentiment, even if it does not solve any structural problems.
Sport therefore probably cannot, on its own, reconcile a deeply divided society, nor can it replace long-term political and social work.
But reducing these moments of collective unity to a mere illusion without consequence would also be excessive.

Perhaps we should accept this more modest reality: sport does not unite a nation sustainably, but it offers, from time to time, the rare opportunity to see itself, briefly, as a whole, before returning to its usual complexities.

sentences: The question regularly arises in public debate: are there topics where humor simply has no place, or can we, as some comedians claim, literally laugh at anything?

Proponents of limitless humor put forward a principled argument: establishing officially prohibited topics would grant humor a power it doesn't actually possess, that of causing harm on its own, regardless of the intent and context in which it is expressed.
From this perspective, it is never the subject itself that poses a problem, but the way it is treated.

However, this position faces a serious objection: the way a subject is treated cannot always be separated from the subject itself, especially when that subject directly affects groups that have historically suffered real discrimination or violence.

Laughing at the suffering of a minority group, even with the declared intention of denouncing an injustice, rarely produces the same effect as laughing, for example, at the universal flaws of the human condition.

A useful distinction might lie in the difference between laughing with and laughing at: the former creates complicity, a shared recognition of a common reality; the latter establishes a distance, an implicit superiority of the laugher over the one being mocked.

Perhaps the real question is not whether we can laugh at everything, which is technically always possible, but rather why we choose to laugh at one thing instead of another, and what this mockery ultimately reveals about the power dynamics between the one who laughs and the one who is laughed at.

sentences: The intuition that our identity relies on the continuity of our memory, this belief that we are today the same individual as yesterday because we remember, subtly governs our ordinary relationship with ourselves, often without us having the opportunity to examine it explicitly.

It is on this intuition, articulated with philosophical clarity since the dawn of modernity, that one of the most influential and contested theories of personal identity rests: the one that makes memory the very criterion of what constitutes us over time.

According to this theory, what makes me, today, the same person as the one who experienced a certain event twenty years ago is neither the continuity of my body, which has completely renewed almost all of its cells since then, nor even an immaterial soul whose existence remains philosophically unverifiable, but the continuous chain of memories that connects me to that past event: I am the one who remembers having lived that, and it is this memorial relationship, rather than any other material or spiritual continuity, that would establish my identity over time.

This theory, appealing in its simplicity, nevertheless faces formidable objections, the first of which concerns precisely what we have established: memory is never a simple faithful deposit but a perpetually reshaped reconstruction, and the memorial criterion of personal identity rests on a foundation that is itself unstable, shifting, never quite the same from one recall to another.

If I am constituted by my memories, and these memories continuously transform, in what precise sense can I still claim to have remained, through these successive reconstructions, a single and same person?

A second, even more radical objection highlights that the memorial chain supposed to ensure the continuity of personal identity contains, for every individual, considerable gaps: no one remembers the entirety of their past life, and the forgotten moments, sometimes by the thousands, do not cease to have been lived by the person we have become.

If memory alone constituted identity, these massive memorial gaps should logically fragment our identity into a multitude of discontinuous segments, separated by the holes in our failing memory; yet we continue, despite these countless gaps, to perceive ourselves as a unique and continuous individual, which suggests that another principle, distinct from simple conscious memory, must intervene to ensure this felt continuity.

Other, older philosophical traditions had proposed alternative answers to this same question, founding identity not on memory but on the continuity of a substance, whether corporeal or spiritual, that is supposed to remain identical over time regardless of what the subject consciously remembers.

These rival theories, now largely abandoned by contemporary philosophy of personal identity, at least had the merit of avoiding the instability of the memorial criterion; but they stumbled upon another difficulty, equally serious: explaining why this substantial continuity, purely material or metaphysical, should count as personal identity in the sense that truly matters to us, that of a subject aware of its own continuity, and not merely as the persistence of an object among others.

These difficulties do not entirely invalidate the initial intuition, but invite us to reformulate it with more nuance: perhaps it is not memory itself, in its precise content and always partial fidelity, that establishes our identity, but the very capacity to tell oneself, to weave, despite the gaps and reconstructions, a continuous narrative of oneself, coherent enough for it to present, to the one who elaborates it, the reassuring appearance of an uninterrupted continuity.

This narrative, never finished, always revised, may nonetheless be no less real: it constitutes, if not the objective proof of a stable underlying identity, at least the psychological condition necessary for an individual to continue to act, to decide, to project themselves into the future as the same subject who committed, yesterday, to such a promise or project.
Are we, then, what we remember having been?

The most honest answer might be the following: we are less what we remember accurately — a requirement that the reconstructive nature of memory makes unattainable anyway — than what we manage, at every moment, to tell about ourselves in a way that is coherent enough to continue living, without unbearable tearing, the same life we started to live.
Identity may not be a fact to be discovered in the folds of a faithful memory, but a work to be pursued, endlessly, in the ever-restarted narrative that each person creates of their own existence.

sentences: No; we are from the continent.
But we have been living here for fifty years.
A feeling of anxiety and fear grips me at the thought of these fifty years spent in this dark hole, so far from the cities where people live.
An old shepherd came back, and we started to eat the only dish for dinner, a thick soup where potatoes, bacon, and cabbage had cooked together.

When the short meal was over, I went to sit in front of the door, my heart tight with the melancholy of the dreary landscape, seized by that distress that sometimes takes travelers on certain sad evenings, in certain desolate places.
It seems that everything is about to end, existence and the universe.
One suddenly perceives the awful misery of life, the isolation of everyone, the emptiness of everything, and the deep solitude of the heart that rocks and deceives itself with dreams until death.

sentences: Has my opponent been involved in shooting?

He remembered the book by Baron de Vaux about pistol shooters, and he read it from cover to cover.
Georges Lamil was not mentioned in it.
But if this man was not a shooter, he wouldn't have immediately accepted this dangerous weapon and these deadly conditions, would he?
He opened, while passing by, a box of Gastinne Renette placed on a side table, and took one of the pistols, then he positioned himself as if to shoot and raised his arm.
But he was trembling from head to toe and the barrel was shaking in all directions.
Then he said to himself:
--It's impossible.
I can't fight like this.

He looked down the barrel at that small, dark, deep hole that spews death; he thought about dishonor, the whispers in the circles, the laughter in the salons, the contempt of women, the allusions in the newspapers, and the insults that the cowards would throw at him.

sentences: Behind the penitents came a tall man.
This man was naked, except for a cloth loincloth to which a large knife hidden in its sheath was attached on the left side; he carried a heavy iron weight on his right shoulder.
This man was the executioner.
He also had sandals tied to the bottom of his legs with cords.
Behind the executioner walked, in the order they were to be executed, first Peppino and then Andrea.
Each was accompanied by two priests.
Neither of them had their eyes covered.
Peppino walked with a fairly steady step; no doubt he had been informed of what was being prepared for him.
Andrea was supported under each arm by a priest.
Both of them occasionally kissed the crucifix that the confessor presented to them.

sentences: Selim, still holding his flaming torch, came to the opening, bowed radiantly under the beam of light, and picked up the sign.
"The master's ring," he said, kissing it, "that's good!"
And turning the torch to the ground, he stepped on it and extinguished it.
The messenger let out a cry of joy and clapped his hands.
At this signal, four soldiers of the seraskier Kourchid rushed in, and Selim fell, pierced by five dagger blows.
Each had delivered his own.
And yet, drunk with their crime, although still pale with fear, they rushed into the underground, searching everywhere for fire and rolling on the sacks of gold.
Meanwhile, my mother grabbed me in her arms, and, agile, bounding through the twists known only to us, she reached a hidden staircase of the kiosk where a terrifying tumult reigned.
The lower halls were completely filled with Kourchid's Tchodoars, that is to say, our enemies.
Just as my mother was about to push the small door, we heard the terrible and threatening voice of the pasha resound.
My mother pressed her eye to the cracks in the boards; an opening happened to be in front of mine, and I looked.

sentences: The notary locked the door and began reading after unsealing the red wax envelope in front of us, the contents of which he did not know.
Suddenly, my friend fell silent, got up, then went to take an old paper from his desk, unfolded it, kissed it longingly, and resumed.
Here is the will of my beloved mother:
"I, the undersigned Anne-Catherine-Geneviève-Mathilde de Croixluce, legitimate wife of Jean-Léopold-Joseph Gontran de Courcils, of sound body and mind, express here my last wishes.
I ask forgiveness from God first, and then from my dear son René, for the act I am about to commit.
I believe my child is big-hearted enough to understand and forgive me.
I have suffered all my life.
I was married for convenience, then despised, unrecognized, oppressed, and constantly deceived by my husband.
I forgive him, but I owe him nothing.
My older sons did not love me, did not spoil me, and treated me hardly as a mother.
I was for them, during my life, what I was meant to be; I owe them nothing after my death.
Blood ties do not exist without the constant, sacred affection of each day.
An ungrateful son is less than a stranger; he is guilty, for he has no right to be indifferent to his mother.

sentences: I was about to take my usual place on the raft when my uncle stopped me with his hand.
"We will only leave tomorrow," he said.
I made the gesture of a man resigned to anything.
"I must not overlook anything," he replied, "and since fate has brought me to this part of the coast, I will not leave without having explored it."
This remark will be understood when it is known that we had returned to the northern shore, but not to the exact spot of our first departure.
Port-Graüben must have been located further west.
It was only reasonable, then, to carefully examine the surroundings of this new landing.
"Let's go explore!" I said.
And, leaving Hans to his tasks, we set off.
The area between the sea's relay points and the foot of the foothills was quite wide; one could walk for half an hour before reaching the rock face.
Our feet crushed countless shells of all shapes and sizes, where the animals of the earliest eras lived.
I also spotted enormous shells; whose diameter often exceeded fifteen feet.
They had belonged to those gigantic glyptodonts from the Pliocene period, of which modern turtles are just a small remnant.
Moreover, the ground was strewn with a large quantity of rocky debris, rounded pebbles shaped by the waves and arranged in successive lines.
I was therefore led to make this observation, that the sea must have once occupied this space.
On the scattered rocks now beyond its reach, the waves had left clear traces of their passage.
This could explain, to a certain extent, the existence of this ocean, located forty leagues below the surface of the globe.
However, in my opinion, this body of water must gradually be lost in the depths of the earth, and it obviously came from the waters of the Ocean, which found their way through some fissure.
Nevertheless, it had to be accepted that this fissure was currently blocked, as this entire cavern, or rather, this immense reservoir, would have filled up in a relatively short time.
Perhaps even this water, having had to struggle against underground fires, had partially vaporized.
This explains the clouds hanging above our heads and the release of this electricity that created storms within the earth's massif.

sentences: Immediately, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade move closer to him, and fearing that he might fall into the sea, they hold him firmly with one hand and then bring him back onto the deck.
I observe, moreover, -- as I have long experience -- that Thomas Roch is in the grip of intense excitement.
He spins around, gestures wildly, and incoherent phrases that are not addressed to anyone spill from his mouth...

It is all too evident that a crisis is imminent -- a crisis similar to the one that seized him during the last evening spent at the Healthful-House pavilion, the consequences of which were so disastrous.
We will need to take hold of him, bring him down to his cabin, where I may be called to give him the special care I am used to...
In the meantime, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade keep a close watch on him.
Presumably, their intention is to let him act, and here is what he does:
After heading towards the main mast, which his eyes have vainly searched for its sails, he reaches it, wraps his arms around it, and tries to shake it as if he wants to bring it down...
And then, seeing his fruitless efforts, what he attempted at the main mast, he will try at the foremast.
His nervousness increases gradually.
Inarticulate cries follow the vague words that escape him...
Suddenly, he rushes towards the port shrouds and clings to them.
I wonder if he is going to leap onto the stays, climbing up to the yardarms...
If we don't stop him, he risks falling onto the deck, or, in a sudden roll, being thrown into the sea...

sentences: However, I was carefully examining these raging waves.

They reached heights of up to fifteen meters over a length of one hundred fifty to one hundred seventy-five meters, and their speed of propagation, half that of the wind, was fifteen meters per second.
Their volume and power increased with the depth of the waters.
I then understood the role of these waves that trap air in their sides and push it down to the depths of the seas where they bring life with oxygen.
Their extreme pressure force — it has been calculated to reach up to three thousand kilograms per square foot of the surface they counteract.
It is such waves that, in the Hebrides, moved a block weighing eighty-four thousand pounds.

It is they who, in the storm of December 23, 1864, after having overturned part of the city of Yedo in Japan, traveling at seven hundred kilometers per hour, broke on the shores of America the same day.
The intensity of the storm increased with the night.
The barometer, like in 1860 in Réunion during a cyclone, fell to 710 millimeters.
At dusk, I saw a large ship struggling on the horizon.
It was steaming under a small power to stay upright in the waves.
It must have been one of the steamers on the routes from New York to Liverpool or Le Havre.
It soon disappeared into the shadows.
At ten o'clock in the evening, the sky was on fire.
The atmosphere was streaked with violent lightning.
I could not bear the brightness, while Captain Nemo, looking directly at them, seemed to draw in the soul of the storm.
A terrible noise filled the air, a complex sound made up of the howls of crashing waves, the roars of the wind, and the cracks of thunder.

The wind was jumping in all directions on the horizon, and the cyclone, starting from the east, returned by way of the north, west, and south, in the opposite direction of the rotating storms of the southern hemisphere.

sentences: Franz offered Albert his sincere compliments; he received them like a man who deserves them.
He had recognized, he said, by certain signs of inimitable elegance, that his beautiful unknown must belong to the highest aristocracy.
He was determined to write to her the next day.
While receiving this confidence, Franz noticed that Albert seemed to have something to ask him, yet he hesitated to make that request.
He insisted, declaring in advance that he was ready to make all the sacrifices within his power for Albert's happiness.
Albert took just the time required for friendly politeness to be persuaded: then finally he admitted to Franz that he would do him a favor by leaving him the carriage all to himself the next day.
Albert attributed the extreme kindness of the beautiful peasant girl in lifting her mask to the absence of his friend.
It is understood that Franz was not selfish enough to stop Albert in the middle of an adventure that promised to be both so enjoyable for his curiosity and so flattering for his self-esteem.

He knew well enough the perfect indiscretion of his worthy friend to be sure that he would keep him informed of every detail of his good fortune; and since, for the past two or three years, he had been traveling all over Italy, he had never even had the chance to initiate such intrigue for himself, so Franz was not displeased to learn how things unfolded in such cases.
He therefore promised Albert that he would be content the next day to watch the spectacle from the windows of the Rospoli palace.
Indeed, the next day he saw Albert going back and forth.
He had a huge bouquet that he had undoubtedly tasked with being the bearer of his love letter.
This possibility became a certainty when Franz saw the same bouquet, notable for a circle of white camellias, in the hands of a charming young woman dressed in pink satin.
So in the evening it was no longer joy, it was delirium.
Albert had no doubt that the beautiful stranger would respond to him in the same way.
Franz went along with his desires by telling him that all this noise was tiring him, and that he had decided to spend the next day revisiting his album and taking notes.

Jasper Hobson was extremely struck by his very affirmative response.
It was indeed possible that the movement of the ice pack was only apparent, and that, on the contrary, Victoria Island, carried by the ice field, was drifting towards the strait.
But this drift, if it existed, could not be observed, could not be estimated, and could not be measured either in longitude or latitude.

In fact, the weather not only remained overcast and unsuitable for observations, but unfortunately, a phenomenon particular to polar regions made it even more obscure and completely restricted the field of vision.
Indeed, precisely at the moment of this thaw, the temperature had dropped several degrees.
A thick fog soon enveloped all these areas of the Arctic Sea, but it was not an ordinary fog.
The ground was soon covered on its surface with a white crust, very distinct from frost, -- the latter being merely a watery vapor that freezes after precipitation.

The very fine particles that made up this fog clung to the trees, shrubs, walls of the fort, and anything that protruded, forming soon a thick layer, bristling with prismatic or pyramidal fibers, the tips of which pointed towards the wind.
Jasper Hobson then recognized this meteorological phenomenon that whalers and winterers have often noted appearing in spring in polar regions.
"This is not a fog," he said to his companions, "it's a frost-rime, a frozen mist, a dense vapor that remains in a completely frozen state."

But, whether fog or frozen mist, the appearance of this meteor was nonetheless regrettable, as it occupied a height of at least one hundred feet above sea level, and so complete was its opacity that, placed three steps apart, two people could not see each other.
The disappointment of the winterers was great.
It seemed that nature did not want to spare them any trouble.

It was at the moment when the thaw was occurring, at the moment when the drifting island was about to be free from the chains that had bound it for so many months, and at the moment when its movements were to be monitored more closely, that this fog came to prevent any observation!

sentences: Every Sunday morning, I go for a one-hour walk in the forest that borders my city.
It's neither a sport nor serious hiking: I walk slowly, without any goal, without a watch.
And every Sunday, the same little miracle happens: I enter the woods with tense shoulders and a full head, and I come out feeling light.
For a long time, I thought it was just a personal impression.
Science says otherwise.
Since the 1980s, researchers, first in Japan, have been seriously studying the effects of the forest on our health.
The results are remarkable.
After a walk in the forest, blood pressure drops, heart rate slows down, and the cortisol level — the main stress hormone — decreases significantly.
The comparison is striking: a walk of the same duration in the city does not produce the same effects.
So it's not just the walk that does you good; it's the forest itself.
How can we explain this?
Several factors complement each other.
First, there is what the forest takes away from us: the noise of traffic, advertising screens, and constant demands.
Our attention, exhausted by the city, can finally rest.
Scientists talk about 'soft attention': looking at the light between the leaves or listening to a bird requires no effort, unlike the constant vigilance that urban life demands.
There is also what the forest gives us.
Trees release natural compounds into the air, and some studies suggest that breathing them in could boost our immune defenses.
These studies still need confirmation, but they are fascinating: the forest is, quite literally, air that heals.
The Japanese have given a lovely name to this practice: shinrin-yoku, or "forest bathing."
The idea is not to cover miles, but to immerse yourself.
Walk slowly.
Stop often.
Touch a tree bark, listen to the wind, breathe deeply.
Leave your phone at the bottom of your bag — or better yet, at home.
Not everyone, it is said, has a forest at their doorstep.
That's true, but the effect also exists, albeit on a smaller scale, in a large park, along a river, under the trees of an avenue.
The principle remains the same: regularly provide your brain with an environment for which it was designed.
We have spent most of our history among trees.
Going back for an hour a week is not escaping the modern world.
It's simply returning home for a moment.

sentences: So, what an idea, he said to himself, my master had to travel during the winter!
Couldn't he wait for the nice season to increase his chances?

But at that moment, when the honest boy was only concerned about the state of the sky and the drop in temperature, Mrs. Aouda was feeling much stronger fears, stemming from a completely different cause.
Indeed, a few travelers had gotten off their carriage and were walking on the platform of the Green River station, waiting for the train to depart.
Now, through the window, the young woman recognized among them Colonel Stamp W.
Proctor, that American who had behaved so rudely towards Phileas Fogg during the meeting in San Francisco.
Mrs. Aouda, not wanting to be seen, leaned back.
This circumstance deeply impressed the young woman.
She had become attached to the man who, as coldly as it was, showed her every day the signs of the most absolute devotion.
She did not understand, of course, the full depth of the feelings her savior inspired in her, and she still only called that feeling gratitude, but unknowingly, there was more to it.
So her heart tightened when she recognized the rude person whom Mr. Fogg would sooner or later confront about his behavior.
Clearly, it was only by chance that Colonel Proctor had ended up on this train, but there he was, and it was essential to prevent Phileas Fogg from seeing his adversary at all costs.

sentences: Jérémie took three steps, then wobbled, stretched out his hands, encountered a wall that held him up, and started walking again, stumbling.

At times, a gust of wind, rushing into the narrow street, pushed him forward, making him run a few steps; then when the force of the storm ceased, he stopped abruptly, having lost his prop, and began to sway again on his drunken, unsteady legs.
He instinctively headed towards his home, like birds returning to their nests.
Finally, he recognized his door and began to feel around for the lock to insert the key.
He couldn't find the hole and swore under his breath.
Then he banged on it with his fist, calling for his wife to come help him:
--Mélina!
Hey!
Mélina!

As he leaned against the door to avoid falling, it gave way, opened up, and Jérémie, losing his support, stumbled into his home, fell flat on his face in the middle of his place, and felt something heavy pass over his body, then flee into the night.
He no longer moved, stunned with fear, distraught, in a devilish terror, haunted by all the mysterious things of the darkness, and he waited a long time without daring to make a move.
But, as he saw that nothing was stirring anymore, a bit of reason returned to him, the muddled reason of a drunkard.
And he sat down, very gently.
He waited a long time again, and finally gathering his courage, he said:
--Mélina!
His wife did not answer.
Then, all of a sudden, a doubt crossed his darkened mind, an indecisive doubt, a vague suspicion.
He did not move; he remained there, sitting on the ground, in the dark, searching for his thoughts, clinging to incomplete and stumbling reflections like his feet.
He asked again:
--Tell me who it was, Mélina?
Tell me who it was.
I won't do anything to you.
He waited.
No voice rose in the darkness.
He was reasoning out loud now.
--I did drink, after all!
I did drink!
It was him who got me drunk like that, that rascal; it was him, so that I wouldn't come back.
I did drink!
And he continued:
--Tell me who it was, Mélina, or I'm going to do something bad.

sentences: In the 2000s, the prediction seemed obvious: with consoles, computers, and soon phones, board games were set to join video cassettes in the museum of lost pastimes.
Twenty years later, the verdict is in — and the opposite has happened.
Board games are experiencing a golden age.
Sales are breaking records year after year, game cafés are opening in all the major cities, and the Cannes festival... of board games attracts tens of thousands of visitors.
What happened?
First, the board game itself has changed.
Forget the memories of endless games and dusty rules.
A new generation of creators — because there are real game authors whose names appear on the boxes — has invented shorter, smarter, and more beautiful games.
Cooperative games, where all players win or lose together, perfect for families tired of arguments.
Party games that make you laugh out loud in five minutes.
Mystery games that you only play once, just like watching a movie.
Today, there is a game for every person, every duration, and every mood.
But the quality of the games doesn't explain everything.
If we are coming back to the tables, it's also, specifically, because of screens.
After entire days spent behind a computer, and then evenings each on their phone, many feel the same lack: being truly together.
Board games offer exactly that.
During a game, we look each other in the eyes, we bluff, we negotiate, we laugh, we gently tease each other.
Try cheating at cards over video conference: it's not the same.
I have an example at home.
Last year, we started 'game Fridays': phones in a basket at the entrance, pizza, and two or three games.
At first, our friends came out of curiosity.
Now, they book their Fridays weeks in advance, and woe to us if we cancel.
The most sought-after moment of the week is the one where there's nothing to watch.
It would be wrong to sharply oppose screens and boards: many players enjoy both, and excellent video games can also be played together.
But the success of board games sends a clear signal about our times.
Technology has given us everything, except one thing: a good reason to sit around a table, face to face, for an hour.
All it took was a cardboard box.

sentences: One morning, as she was returning, she suddenly thought she saw the long barrel of a rifle aimed at her.
It was sticking out obliquely over the edge of a small barrel, half-buried among the grass, on the edge of a ditch.
Emma, ready to faint from terror, moved forward anyway, and a man emerged from the barrel, like those jack-in-the-boxes that spring up from the bottom of their boxes.
He was wearing gaiters buckled up to his knees, his cap pulled down over his eyes, with trembling lips and a red nose.
It was Captain Binet, lying in wait for wild ducks.
You should have called out from a distance! he shouted.
When you see a rifle, you must always warn someone.

The tax collector was trying to hide the fear he had just felt; because a prefectural decree had prohibited duck hunting except from a boat, Mr. Binet, despite his respect for the law, was in violation.
So he believed he could hear the gamekeeper approaching every minute.
But this worry only spoiled his enjoyment, and all alone in his barrel, he congratulated himself on his happiness and his mischief.

sentences: Well then, said the count, aren't you getting out, Mr. Bertuccio? So you're staying in the car then?

Bertuccio rushed through the door and offered his shoulder to the count, who this time leaned on it and went down the three steps of the footboard one by one.
Knock, said the count, and announce me.
Bertuccio knocked, the door opened, and the concierge appeared.
What is it? he asked.
--It's your new master, good man, said the footman.
And he handed the concierge the letter of recognition given by the notary.
So the house is sold? asked the concierge, and is it Mr. who is coming to live here?
--Yes, my friend, said the count, and I will make sure you won't regret your former master.

--Oh! sir, said the concierge, I won't have much to regret, because we see him very rarely; it's been more than five years since he came, and he certainly did well to sell a house that brought him absolutely nothing.

sentences: Everything having been agreed upon, from this day forward, the preparations for the perilous expedition were carried out quickly.
The men had bravely accepted that they had six hundred miles to cover under these conditions.
Sergeant Long was in charge of the work, while Jasper Hobson, the two hunters, and Mrs. Paulina Barnett frequently went to assess the state of the icefield.
Kalumah accompanied them most often, and his advice, based on experience, could be very useful to the lieutenant.

sentences: Nothing seemed changed to me.
The castle still soaked its grayish walls in the pond at the entrance of the small town; and the inn was the same, although repaired, renovated, with a more modern look.
Upon entering, I was greeted by two young Breton women of eighteen, fresh and kind, clad in their tight wool vests, wearing silver caps with large embroidered plaques on their ears.
It was around six o'clock in the evening.
I sat down to dinner, and as the owner himself hurried to serve me, fate perhaps made me say: "Did you know the former owners of this house?
I spent about ten days here thirty years ago now.
I speak to you from afar."
He replied: "They were my parents, sir."
Then I told him on what occasion I had stopped, how I had been held up by a friend's illness.
He did not let me finish.
"Oh! I remember perfectly. I was then fifteen or sixteen.
You slept in the back room and your friend in the one I have made mine, on the street."
It was only then that the very vivid memory of the little maid came back to me.
I asked, "Do you remember a nice little servant that your father had back then, who had, if my memory serves me right, pretty blue eyes and fresh teeth?"

Then, seeing the downstairs room empty as usual and merely watched over by his dog, he called for his wife.
--Hey! Carconte, he said, that worthy priest didn't deceive us; the diamond was real.

--What are you saying? asked the woman, paler than a corpse.
--I'm saying that the diamond was real, and here is a gentleman, one of the top jewelers in Paris, who is ready to give us fifty thousand francs for it.

In the meantime, sir, please have a seat, and since the weather is heavy, I will go get something to refresh you.

sentences: Noirtier's gaze remained fixed and firm, as if to say that a promise was not enough for him; then he shifted from the face to the hand.
"Do you want me to swear, sir?" asked Maximilien.
--"Yes," replied the paralytic with the same solemnity, "I want you to."
Morrel understood that the old man placed great importance on this oath.
He extended his hand.
"On my honor," he said, "I swear to wait for what you decide in order to act against Mr. d'Épinay.
--"Good," the old man said with his eyes.
--"Now, sir," asked Morrel, "do you order me to leave?
--"Yes.
--"Without seeing Miss Valentine again?
Morrel signaled that he was ready to obey.
Now, continued Morrel, would you allow, sir, for your son to kiss you just as your daughter did a moment ago!
There was no mistaking the expression in Noirtier's eyes.
The young man placed his lips on the old man's forehead in the same spot where the young girl had placed hers.
Then he saluted the old man once more and left.
In the courtyard, he found the old servant, informed by Valentine; he was waiting for Morrel and guided him through the twists of a dark corridor that led to a small door opening onto the garden.

Once there, Morrel reached the gate, and through the trellis, he was at the top of the wall in an instant, and by means of his ladder, he was in the alfalfa enclosure in a second, where his cabriolet was still waiting for him.

He got back in, and overwhelmed by so many emotions, but with a lighter heart, he returned around midnight to rue Meslay, threw himself onto his bed, and slept as if he had been plunged into a deep intoxication.

sentences: Oh! oh! said the brigadier, old fox raised in the tricks of the state, a bad sign that a door is open! I would prefer it locked with three bolts!
Indeed, the small letter and the pin left by Andrea on the table confirmed or rather supported the sad truth.
Andrea had escaped.
We say supported, because the brigadier was not the kind of man to be convinced by a single piece of evidence.
He looked around him, peered under the bed, pulled back the curtains, opened the cupboards, and finally stopped at the fireplace.
Thanks to Andrea's precautions, no trace of his passage remained in the ashes.
However, it was an exit, and in the circumstances they found themselves in, any exit warranted serious investigation.
The brigadier had a bundle and straw brought to him, stuffed the fireplace as he would have done with mortar, and set it on fire.
The fire made the brick walls crack; an opaque column of smoke shot up through the flues and rose to the sky like the dark jet of a volcano, but he did not see the prisoner fall, as he had expected.

This is because Andrea, from his youth struggling against society, was worth a gendarme, even if that gendarme had been promoted to the respectable rank of brigadier; anticipating the fire, he had reached the roof and was huddled against the pipe.
For a moment he had some hope of being saved, for he heard the brigadier calling the two gendarmes and shouting to them loudly:
He's not there anymore.

But as he gently stretched his neck, he saw that the two gendarmes, instead of stepping back, as would be natural at the first announcement, he saw, let’s say, that on the contrary the two gendarmes were becoming even more attentive.

sentences: Did you never have any complaints about him? asked the governor of the jailer in charge of bringing the abbé's provisions.
Never, Mr. Governor, replied the jailer, never, not ever! On the contrary: he used to entertain me a lot by telling me stories; one day when my wife was ill, he even gave me a recipe that cured her.
Ah! ah! said the doctor, I didn't know I was dealing with a colleague; I hope, Mr. Governor, he added with a laugh, that you will treat him accordingly.
Yes, yes, rest assured, he will be decently buried in the newest sack we can find; are you satisfied?
Must we carry out this last formality in front of you, sir? asked one of the clerks.
Of course, but let’s hurry, I can't stay in this room all day.

New comings and goings were heard; a moment later, the sound of crumpled cloth reached Dantès's ears, the bed creaked on its springs, a heavy step like that of a man lifting a burden settled on the stone, then the bed creaked again under the weight being returned to it.
"See you tonight," said the governor.
Will there be a mass? asked one of the officers.

Impossible, replied the governor; the castle chaplain came to ask me yesterday for a leave to take a short trip to Hyères, I told him about all my prisoners during that time; the poor abbé should have taken his time, and he would have had his requiem.

Hyères, said the doctor with the irreverence familiar to people in his profession, he is a man of the Church: God will take the state into account, and will not give hell the wicked pleasure of sending him a priest.

sentences: And he counted fifteen thousand francs in gold and thirty thousand francs in banknotes on the table.
--Wait for me to light the lamp, said Carconte, it's no longer bright, and we might make a mistake.
Indeed, night had fallen during this discussion, and with the night, the storm that had been threatening for half an hour.
One could hear the distant rumble of thunder; but neither the jeweler, nor Caderousse, nor Carconte seemed to care, as they were all three possessed by the demon of greed.
I myself felt a strange fascination at the sight of all this gold and all these banknotes.
It seemed to me that I was dreaming, and, as often happens in a dream, I felt chained to my place.
Caderousse counted and recounted the gold and the banknotes, then he passed them to his wife, who counted and recounted them in turn.

Meanwhile, the jeweler was making the diamond sparkle under the lamp's rays, and the diamond was throwing flashes that made him forget those that, as precursors of the storm, were beginning to light up the windows.
--Well, is the count correct? asked the jeweler.
--Yes, said Caderousse; give me the wallet and look for a bag, Carconte.

Carconte went to a cupboard and returned with an old leather wallet, from which some greasy letters were taken out and replaced with the banknotes, and a bag that contained two or three coins of six livres, which probably made up the entire fortune of the miserable household.
--There, said Caderousse, although you may have raised about ten thousand francs for us, would you like to have dinner with us? It's with good heart.

sentences: As soon as this property is purchased, I will have relays every ten leagues along the Northern and Southern routes.
Your Excellency can count on me.
The count made a sign of satisfaction, went down the steps, jumped into his carriage, which, driven at a trot by the magnificent team, only stopped in front of the banker’s hotel.
Danglars was presiding over a committee appointed for a railway when he was informed of the visit from the Count of Monte Cristo.
The meeting, by the way, was almost over.
In the name of the count, he stood up.

Gentlemen, he said, addressing his colleagues, several of whom were honorable members of one chamber or the other, forgive me for leaving you like this; but can you imagine that the house of Thomson and French in Rome has sent me a certain Count of Monte-Cristo, opening an unlimited credit for him at my place.
This is the funniest joke that my correspondents from abroad have ever allowed themselves to make at my expense.
Indeed, as you understand, curiosity has seized me and still holds me; I went this morning to see the so-called count.
If he were a real count, you understand he wouldn't be so rich.
The gentleman was not available.
What do you think? Are these not the manners of a highness or a beautiful woman that Master Monte-Cristo is putting on?
By the way, the house located on the Champs-Élysées that belongs to him, I inquired about it, seemed proper to me.
But an unlimited credit, Danglars replied with his nasty smile, makes the banker where the credit is opened quite demanding.
So I can't wait to see our man.
I feel like I'm being mystified.
But they don't know over there who they are dealing with; he who laughs last, laughs best.

sentences: At the creaking of the massive locks, at the cry of the rusty hinges turning on their pivots, Dantès, crouched in a corner of his cell, where he received with indescribable happiness the thin ray of daylight filtering through a narrow barred window, lifted his head.

At the sight of an unknown man, illuminated by two jailers holding torches, to whom the governor was speaking with his hat in hand, accompanied by two soldiers, Dantès guessed what it was about, and, finally seeing an opportunity to implore a higher authority, leapt forward with his hands clasped.
The soldiers immediately crossed their bayonets, for they believed that the prisoner was rushing towards the inspector with ill intentions.
The inspector himself took a step back.
Dantès saw that he had been presented as a man to be feared.

Then, he gathered in his gaze all that the heart of man can contain of gentleness and humility, and expressing himself with a kind of pious eloquence that astonished those present, he tried to touch the soul of his visitor.
The inspector listened to Dantès's speech until the end, then turning to the governor:
"He will turn to devotion," he said in a low voice; "he is already inclined to gentler feelings.
See, fear is having its effect on him; he recoiled before the bayonets; now, a madman does not recoil before anything: I have made some very curious observations on this subject at Charenton."
Then, turning back to the prisoner:
"In summary," he said, "what do you ask for?

--I ask what crime I have committed; I ask that judges be appointed for me; I ask that my trial be conducted; I finally ask that I be shot if I am guilty, but also that I be set free if I am innocent.
Are you well-fed? asked the inspector.
Yes, I believe so; I don't really know.

But that matters little; what should matter, not only to me, the unfortunate prisoner, but also to all the officials administering justice, and even to the king who governs us, is that an innocent person is not the victim of an infamous denunciation and does not die behind bars cursing his executioners.
You are quite humble today, said the governor; you haven't always been like this.
You spoke very differently, my dear friend, on the day you wanted to knock out your guard.

sentences: I would add that this man was proud, that his firm and calm gaze seemed to reflect lofty thoughts, and that from this whole, from the homogeneity of expressions in the gestures of the body and face, following the observation of physiognomists, resulted an undeniable sincerity.
I felt "involuntarily" reassured in his presence, and I had a good feeling about our meeting.
Whether this man was thirty-five or fifty years old, I couldn't say.

He was tall, with a broad forehead, a straight nose, a distinctly shaped mouth, magnificent teeth, and fine, elongated hands, eminently "psychic" to use a term from chiromancy, meaning worthy of serving a high and passionate soul.
This man certainly represented the most admirable type I had ever encountered.
A particular detail, his eyes, slightly spaced apart, could simultaneously take in nearly a quarter of the horizon.
This ability, as I later verified, was accompanied by a vision power even greater than that of Ned Land.

When this stranger focused on an object, the line of his eyebrows furrowed, his wide eyelids drew closer together to encircle the pupils of his eyes and thus narrow the extent of his field of vision, and he looked!

What a gaze! How it magnified objects diminished by distance! How it penetrated to your very soul! How it pierced through those liquid layers, so opaque to our eyes, and how it read to the depths of the seas!...

The two strangers, wearing berets made of sea otter fur and dressed in sea boots made of seal skin, wore garments of a particular fabric that accentuated their waists and allowed for great freedom of movement.
The larger of the two, obviously the captain, examined us with great attention, without saying a word.
Then, turning to his companion, he conversed with him in a language I couldn't recognize.
It was a sonorous, harmonious, flexible idiom, whose vowels seemed to be subjected to a very varied accentuation.
The other responded with a nod and added two or three perfectly incomprehensible words.
Then, with his gaze, he seemed to question me directly.
I replied, in good French, that I did not understand his language; but he did not seem to understand me, and the situation became quite awkward.

sentences: Victoria Island was then floating in the largest part of the Bering Sea, six hundred miles from the first Aleutians and over two hundred miles from the nearest coast to the east.
Its movement was still occurring at a relatively considerable speed.
However, assuming it did not suffer any decrease, it would still need at least three weeks to reach the southern barrier of the Bering Sea.
Could this island last until then, whose base was thinning each day under the action of the already warm waters, averaging fifty degrees Fahrenheit (10° Celsius above zero)?
Could its ground open up at any moment?
Lieutenant Hobson was urging the construction of the raft with all his might, the lower frame of which was already floating on the lagoon's waters.
Mac Nap wanted to give this device a great solidity so that it could withstand the shocks of the sea for a long time, if necessary.
Indeed, it was to be assumed that, if he did not encounter any whaling ship in the Bering area, he would drift to the Aleutian Islands, and a long stretch of sea remained to be crossed.
However, Victoria Island had not yet experienced any significant change in its overall configuration.

Reconnaissances were being made daily, but the explorers ventured out only with extreme caution, as at any moment a fracture in the ground or a fragmentation of the island could isolate them from the common center.
Those who set out like this could always be feared to never return.
The deep gash located near Cape Michel, which the winter cold had sealed, had gradually reopened.
It now extended for a mile inland to the dry bed of the small river.
One could even fear that it would follow this bed, which, already carved out, was thinning the ice crust.
In that case, the entire area between Cape Michel and Barnett Port, limited to the west by the riverbed, would have disappeared — that is to say, a huge piece, covering several square miles.
Lieutenant Hobson therefore advised his companions not to venture there unnecessarily, as a strong movement of the sea was enough to detach this significant part of the island's territory.

I meet people I know.
At one o'clock, it's over.

The cars come back.
And we have to wait for next Wednesday.

sentences: There is a small social skill that many have never learned: to refuse clearly.
An invitation that doesn't interest us, a favor that we don't have time to do, a request that is too much.
Rather than saying no, many people reluctantly accept, or come up with a complicated excuse, or vaguely promise to get out of it at the moment.
These strategies are problematic.
Accepting what we don't want creates resentment, often unfairly directed at the person who asked.
Making up an excuse creates a risk: the excuse can be disproven, and you then have to remember it.
Vaguely promising simply postpones the discomfort.
A clear refusal is actually more respectful.
It allows the other person to organize themselves differently, without false hope.
The main difficulty is not saying no, but resisting the urge to justify yourself too much.
The more explanations you add, the more you seem to be seeking permission, and the more you open the door to negotiation.
Simple phrases are often enough.
"Thank you for thinking of me, but I won't be able to."
"That's nice, but I'll pass this time."
These phrases are complete.
They don't need to be elaborated on.
If you want, you can suggest something else: "Not tonight, but another day with pleasure."
The refusal then focuses on the specific request, not on the person.
What surprises those who try it the most is the reaction of others.
Almost no one gets offended.
Most people accept an honest no much better than a hesitant yes.

sentences: I have nothing to hide, so surveillance doesn't bother me.
This argument, undoubtedly the most common against concerns about privacy, has a certain common sense to it.
If you aren't doing anything wrong, why fear being watched?
Only the guilty would have to fear being observed.
This idea is so common that it seems obvious.
However, it rests on several confusions, and examining it closely is enough to reveal its fragility.
The first confusion equates privacy with hiding a wrongdoing.
However, protecting one's intimacy has never meant hiding misdeeds.

We close the bathroom door, we lower our voices for a secret, we keep our most intimate feelings to ourselves — not because we are doing something wrong, but because there exists a sphere that belongs only to us.
Privacy is not the shadow where the guilty hide; it is the personal space of every individual, the acknowledgment that a part of us is not for others to see.
Having nothing to hide does not mean accepting to show everything.
The second confusion assumes that what is innocent today will always remain so and can never turn against us.
This forgets that perception can change in nature.

An innocuous piece of information under one regime can become compromising under another; a commonplace opinion today can be condemned tomorrow; data collected for a specific purpose can be redirected for another.
Revealing your traces while relying on the current goodwill of those who hold them is to make an imprudent bet on the future, over which we have no control regarding the actors or their intentions.
The third confusion, more subtle, reduces everything to the individual who speaks.
"I have nothing to hide": but privacy is not just an individual matter.
Even if everyone, for their own sake, accepted being observed, the accumulation of data from all gives a few individuals considerable power, the effects of which weigh on society as a whole.
And there are people for whom the protection of privacy is not a luxury but a vital necessity: the dissident, the journalist, the victim trying to escape their tormentor.
By renouncing privacy because "we have nothing to hide," we weaken a protection that others desperately need.
There is finally something troubling about the argument itself.
Saying 'I have nothing to hide' already means accepting the idea that scrutiny is legitimate, and that it falls to each person to prove their innocence by exposing themselves.
But why should I have to justify my right to privacy?
It is up to surveillance to justify itself, not to private life.

Shifting the burden, demanding that everyone show their clean hands, is already conceding the essential: the principle that a person has a right, by default, to a part of their existence that is shielded from view.
The argument of 'nothing to hide' is therefore much weaker than it seems.
It confuses intimacy and guilt, recklessly bets on the future, forgets the collective dimension, and shifts the burden of justification.
Defending privacy is not the reflex of someone with shameful secrets; it is recognizing that a free existence needs both shadow and light, for oneself and for others.

sentences: The end justifies the means.
This phrase, often quoted to be condemned, expresses one of the most distressing problems of action morality: can one do evil for the sake of a greater good?
Is it permissible to resort to condemnable means if the pursued goal is good, or even necessary?
This question is not academic; it arises in real action, especially in politics, where it is often claimed that one must do evil for a greater good.
Answering it requires untangling what the phrase mixes, and resisting two overly simple answers.
The first simple answer is the one that unreservedly approves the phrase: yes, the end justifies the means, and if the goal is good, any means to achieve it is legitimate.
This position, often attributed to those in power, has an appearance of realism: in action, it says, one cannot afford scruples, one must be effective, and only the result matters.

But taken to its extreme, this position is monstrous: it justifies all crimes in the name of the ends they would serve, it abolishes any moral limit, and it makes the goal a universal justification for any means.

If the end really justified all means, then the worst atrocities would be permitted in the name of supposedly good goals, and history shows where this logic leads: to crimes committed in the name of brighter tomorrows, to horrors justified by the ends they were supposed to serve.

The second simple, opposing response absolutely condemns the formula: no, the end never justifies the means, and certain acts are forbidden regardless of their consequences, no matter what good they might produce.
This position, which is more noble, asserts that there are limits that nothing can override, acts that no end could justify, and a dignity of the person that cannot be sacrificed for any purpose.
It has on its side moral firmness, the refusal of the slope that justifies everything by the ends.

But it also encounters a difficulty: for there seem to be cases where absolutely refusing any condemnable means would lead to worse consequences, where inflexibility regarding the means would sacrifice immense goods.
Should we allow innocents to perish rather than transgress a rule?
The absolutism of means can also lead to results that are hard to accept.

Between these two positions, moral reflection has sought more nuanced paths, recognizing the complexity of the problem without yielding to either the cynicism that justifies everything or an absolutism that ignores the consequences.

We can distinguish according to the means: some are so radically contrary to dignity — torture, the murder of innocents — that no end could justify them, while others, lesser ones, can be weighed against the ends.
We can distinguish according to the ends: not all are equal, and the invoked good must be real, certain, proportionate, not a distant and hypothetical pretext.

We can recognize that action sometimes involves tragedy, those situations where every choice is culpable, where one cannot act without getting their hands dirty, and where one must assume the share of evil in their action without absolving themselves.
For it is perhaps there that the deepest truth about this question lies: in the recognition of the tragic nature of action.
Those who act, especially in public affairs, sometimes face situations where every option involves harm, where one must choose the lesser evil without that lesser evil ceasing to be an evil.

Lucidity then consists not in persuading oneself that the end justifies the means, erasing the fault, nor in refusing to act in the name of purity, but in acknowledging the harmful aspect of one's action while recognizing it as such.

The responsible man of action is neither the cynic who believes he is justified by his ends, nor the pure one who refuses to get his hands dirty; it is the one who, sometimes forced to use dubious means, bears the weight of it without absolving himself, who retains a sense of fault even when he believes he must commit it.
The phrase 'the end justifies the means' is therefore both false and incomplete.
False, if it means that the goal erases the nature of the means, that anything is permitted in the name of the ends; that would abolish all morality.
Incomplete, because it ignores the complexity: that some means are absolutely forbidden, that others can be weighed, that action sometimes involves tragedy.

True wisdom is neither to justify everything by the ends, nor to ignore the consequences in the name of an abstract purity, but to hold together the respect for absolute limits, the weighing of consequences, and the tragic lucidity that acknowledges the harmful aspect of action without ever absolving itself.
The end does not justify the means; but it does not render them indifferent either; and acting morally, in an imperfect world, often means bearing the weight of this rift.
