sentences: Beauty will save the world.
This phrase from a great novelist, as famous as it is enigmatic, keeps coming up, cited fervently, even though we don't always know what it means.
How could beauty, which seems so powerless, so foreign to the forces that govern the world, save it?
What would it save it from, and by what power?
The phrase initially appears to be a beautiful empty word, a pious wish of an aesthete.
But perhaps it contains a deep intuition, worth exploring, about the power of beauty and what our world needs saving from.
First, we must dispel any misunderstandings.

The phrase obviously does not mean that the contemplation of beautiful things would solve the world's problems, that art could replace political or moral action, or that beauty would be a solution to concrete miseries.
Such an interpretation would be naive, and even indecent: beauty has never fed the hungry nor stopped tyrants.
If the phrase has any meaning, it is not one of the practical effectiveness of beauty, which has none.
It is elsewhere that we must seek what beauty could 'save', in a realm that is not that of action, but of what underlies or precedes it.

Perhaps beauty saves in that it testifies, against the evil and ugliness of the world, that something else is possible, that there exists a value, an order, a harmony that cannot be reduced to chaos, violence, or self-interest.
In a world filled with moral and physical ugliness, beauty is like a promise, a sign that evil does not have the final word, that there is something of worth, that elevates, that transcends.

It does not combat evil directly, but it preserves from despair those who, without it, might believe that everything is just ugliness; it keeps alive the idea that there exists a value, without which the very struggle against evil would lose its meaning.
Beauty perhaps saves in that it keeps open the dimension of value, without which there would be nothing to save.
There is more.
Beauty could save in that it transforms the one who contemplates it, opening them to something beyond their own interest, pulling them out of self-absorption.

The experience of beauty is disinterested: in the presence of what is beautiful, we do not seek to possess, to use, to benefit; we contemplate, we forget ourselves, we open ourselves to what transcends us.
This experience educates us to a relationship with the world that is not one of greed, possession, or utility; it teaches us to value what is useless, to respect what is valuable in itself.
In this sense, beauty could 'save' by forming in us a disposition — disinterestedness, contemplation, respect for what transcends our interest — which the world, precisely, sorely lacks.
But we must be careful not to idealize beauty, as if it were always on the side of good.

For beauty can also seduce, deceive, and serve evil; there are moral uglinesses that adorn themselves with beauty, criminal powers that have cultivated superb art, and aesthetic seductions employed for the worst.
Beauty is not necessarily moral; it can enchant, divert, and make us accept the unacceptable under beautiful appearances.
To believe that beauty would always save, that it would inherently be on the side of good, would be a dangerous naivety, as history proves.
Beauty is ambivalent, like all power; it can elevate or seduce, open us to good or divert us from it.
What can we conclude from this meditation?
Perhaps the formula, rather than an assertion, is a question or a fragile hope.
Beauty will not automatically save the world, nor with an effectiveness it does not have, nor because it is always on the side of good.
But it can, if we know how to welcome it, preserve within us the dimension of value, open us to selflessness, and testify that something other than ugliness and evil is possible.

In this precise and limited sense, it participates in what could save the world — not alone, not by magic, but as one of the signs and one of the forces that keep alive the idea that there is something worthwhile, and that deserves to be saved.
Beauty does not save the world; but a world that has lost even the sense of beauty would undoubtedly already be lost.
Perhaps that is what the formula says: not that beauty is enough, but that without it, nothing would suffice.

sentences: Some songs instantly take me back to when I was fifteen, as if by magic.
Just hearing the first notes of a song I listened to at that age brings back specific feelings: the smell of my teenage room, the excitement before a party, a long-forgotten heartbreak.
Researchers explain this phenomenon by saying that adolescence is a time when the brain forms particularly strong memories.
The music we listen to at that time becomes linked to very strong emotions.
I've noticed that I still listen, even today, almost exclusively to the bands I liked at sixteen.
My musical tastes have hardly changed since then.
My son is now the age I was back then, and he listens to completely different music that I don't always understand.
One evening, I asked him to explain what he liked about one of his favorite songs.
He shrugged: "It's just good, dad, I don't know how to explain it."
This answer made me smile; it's exactly what I would say at his age when my own parents asked me the same question.
Sometimes I wonder if, in twenty years, these current songs will remind him of this period of his life, just like mine remind me of mine.
There's something reassuring about this idea: the music we love at fifteen may never really leave us, even when everything else changes.

sentences: I reassured him as best I could, glad to have come that very evening and to witness the spectacle of this superstitious terror.
I told stories, and I managed to calm almost everyone down.
Near the hearth, an old, almost blind, mustachioed dog—one of those dogs that resemble people we know—was sleeping with his nose in his paws.

Outside, the fierce storm battered the little house, and through a narrow window, a sort of peephole near the door, I suddenly saw a jumble of trees being tossed by the wind in the light of great flashes of lightning.
Despite my efforts, I could tell that a deep terror held these people, and every time I stopped speaking, all ears listened intently.

Tired of witnessing these foolish fears, I was about to ask to go to bed when the old guard suddenly jumped from his chair, grabbed his gun again, and stammered in a bewildered voice: "There it is! There it is!
I can hear it!"
The two women fell to their knees in their corners, hiding their faces; and the sons picked up their axes again.

I was about to try to calm them once more when the sleeping dog suddenly woke up and, lifting his head, stretching his neck, looking towards the fire with his almost extinguished eye, let out one of those mournful howls that make travelers shudder in the countryside at night.
All eyes turned to him; he remained still now, standing on his legs as if haunted by a vision, and he began to howl at something invisible, unknown, and surely dreadful, as all his fur bristled.
The guard, pale, shouted: "He senses it! He senses it! It was there when I killed it."
And the bewildered women both began to howl along with the dog.

sentences: I was crossing the vast dunes south of Ouargla.
It is one of the strangest countries in the world.
You know the smooth sand, the straight sand of the endless beaches of the Ocean.
Well! Imagine the Ocean itself turned to sand in the midst of a hurricane; picture a silent storm of motionless waves in yellow dust.
These waves are as high as mountains, uneven, different, rising just like raging seas, but even larger, and streaked like watered silk.
On this furious, silent, and motionless sea, the blazing sun of the south pours down its relentless and direct flame.
One must climb these golden ash waves, descend, climb again, climb endlessly, without rest and without shade.
The horses are gasping, sinking up to their knees, and sliding down the other side of the surprising hills.
We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this burning desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained still, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these lost lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic roll.
The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said, in his language: "Death is upon us."
And suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, that elusive drum continually filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, true fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four sand mountains, while the unknown echo cast upon us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it meant to be afraid; I realized it even more clearly another time...
